speechtext:
Id the absence of the Prime Minister I beg leave to move, seconded by the Minister of Railways and Canals:
That on Saturday, the fourteenth day of June instant, the House shall meet at three o'clock in the afternoon, the order of precedence being the same as on Friday, and that on and after Monday, the sixteen day of June instant until the end of the present session, the House shall meet at eleven o'clock in the morning of each day except Sundays, and that in addition

to the usual intermission at six o'clock, p.m., there shall he also an intermission every d from one to three o'clock, p.m.
He said: I am not sure whether or not the Prime Minister has spoken to the leader of the Opposition respecting the matter, but as the leader of the Government is not in his seat I have taken the opportunity of presenting the resolution.

I presume that in the absence of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance would not care to give a decision in this matter. I have had no notice of the resolution except that it appears in the Votes and Proceedings, and I hear that many hon. gentlemen, at all events of those sitting on this side, would not be agreeable to commencing Saturday sittings as early as the 14th instant. This is Thursday, and many hon. gentlemen are away. As we are all public men there is no objection to mentioning that in the neighbouring province an election is in progress and quite a few members are absent and taking part in it to whom it will be a convenience to have next Saturday. Possibly the motion might stand until opportunity has been afforded for further consultation with the Prime Minister himself when he is present. I would like to say to the Minister of Finance that the practice has been, I think, that before recourse was had to Saturday and morning sittings the balance of the (Government's legislative programme shall be brought down and disclosed, for the reason that when these sittings commence there is none too much time for deliberation upon any question before the House. I hope, therefore, that before we enter upon these additional sittings that the Prime Minister will disclose what the Government's programme for the remainder of the session will he.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I had expected that the Prime Minister would have been in his seat at three o'clock this afternoon, but in his momentary absence I would suggest that the resolution stand as a notice of motion. It can he disposed of to-morrow, and in the interval I have no doubt the Prime Minister will speak to the leader of the Opposition with respect to it.
iHfon. Mr. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's): Might I suggest a further consideration: In the present stage of the work of the Committees of the House, I doubt if much progress can be made by having Saturday sittings. There is the greatest difficulty now in getting meetings of com-

mittees, and if we are to meet on Saturday as usual I am afraid it will add to the difficulties of the committee work. I merely offer that as a suggestion for the consideration of the Acting Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing the House on this important subject from the somewhat precarious, but nevertheless very interesting and, latterly, much coveted location (the cross benches), I wish to make a brief reference to the question of political independence which was raised in the debate on The Address by .my hon. friend the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Hon. Mr. Fielding) when there was a slight apparent divergence of opinion between him and me. He seemed to me to plead rather strongly for party government as being necessary for. political accomplishment. I interjected a question as to whether Mr. Gobden was not a proof to the contrary. I still think that I was correct in that, and I am of opinion that a good many more proofs can be adduced that political accomplishment is very often great along the line of .political independence.
We all know what happened in the case of Cobden. He declared again and again in the British House of Commons that he was neither a Whig nor a Tory, but a Free Trader. He converted the greatest administrator-and, some would say, the greatest statesman-of the 19th century to his views, and on the occasion of those views being passed into law the pre-eminence of Cob-den's position in the matter was given the

most generous recognition by Sir Robert Peel himself in these words:
The name which ought to be, and will be, associated with the success of these measures is the name of one who, acting, I believe, from pure and disinterested motives, has with untiring energy made appeals to our reason and has enforced those appeals with an eloquence the more to be admired because it was unaffected and unadorned ; the name which ought to be associated with the success of those measures is the name of Richard Cobden.
' The events of that day led to the creation of a party which was known in England as the party of the Peelites-the most distinguished subsequent member of which was, of course, Mr. Gladstone.
At a later period of English history, at the time when Mr. Gladstone himself endeavoured to pass Home Rule, he was left by a body of the most distinguished parliamentarians, both in the House of Commons and in the House of Lords. The names which occur to one are those of Bright, Chamberlain, and the late Duke of Devonshire. These men, not only outstanding, but by far the most outstanding of his followers, could not see eye to eye with him, and left him, and up to now they have had the better of the argument as between themselves and their great leader, because Home Rule is not yet an accomplished fact.
At a still later period, when the Conservative party of England under the brilliant leadership of Mr. Chamberlain was tempted to go back on free trade principles, which had for a generation or more been held by both parties in Great Britain, again the then Duke of Devonshire led a number of distinguished men to dissent from his party and take an independent line, which at that time had a marked effect in defeating Mr. Chamberlain's proposal to take Great Britain back to protection.
I need not confine myself to the other side of the Atlantic for instances of independence in politics having a marked effect upon the fortunes of a nation. Is it not the case, Sir, that at Confederation itself the very greatest men of both parties suppressed their party convictions for the meantime and joined in one Government for the purpose of carrying through Confederation?
And a still later case, which surely ought to appeal to my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), is that of the Liberal Unionists of Canada, who left the .most distinguished political leader probably that Canada has ever had because it was their misfortune, from the personal point of view, not to be able to agree with him upon the methods by which the great war was to be carried
to a successful conclusion. That case ought, I say, to appeal most strongly to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, because by length of parliamentary experience and by the greatness of his parliamentary ability he was the most distinguished member of these Liberal Unionists.
My hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) said something yesterday about heroism and popularity being the rewards under certain conditions of Liberal independence.
If that be true, in a good many cases they have been the only rewards that have come to the Independents. The road of an Independent in Canada has usually been particularly thorny, because rarely does Canada elect Independents to Parliament. In the case of Sir Robert Peel, the result of the independent lead which he gave the British nation and by which he accomplished the greatest economic reform of the century for his country, and, I believe, the greatest economic reform of the world for all time, was told in graphic language by himself at the end of the speech from which I have already made a quotation. Those of us who remember our English history at all know that Peel broke his party to accomplish his reform, and that he had to retire from public life and from the Premiership of Great Britain as a consequence. In closing his speech he said:
In relinquishing power, I shall leave a name, severely censured I fear toy many who, on public grounds, deeply regret the severance of party ties-deeply regret that severance, not from personal motives, tout from the firm conviction that fidelity to party engagements-the existence and maintenance of a great party, constitutes a powerful instrument of Government. I shall surrender power, severely censured also, toy others who, from no interested motive, adhere to the principle of protection, considering the maintenance of it to be essential to the welfare and interests of the country. I shall leave a name execrated by every monopolist who, from less honourable motives, clamours for protection because it conduces to his own immediate benefit: tout It may toe that I shall leave a name sometimes remembered with expressions of good-will In the abode of those whose lot it is to labour and to earn their daily (bread toy the sweat of their brow, when they shall recruit their exhausted strength with abundant and untaxed food, the sweeter because it is no longer leavened toy a sense of Injustice.
I have ventured thus far on that topic, because I think the House will agree with me that it has some bearing upon the particular events through which we are passing at the present moment in this country.
In looking at the matters of finance and

trade which have been brought to our attention as they are annually in the Budget, I want to say that not only this, but all other matters that come before Parliament and before public men generally for consideration should be viewed in the bright light from the fields of France and Flanders that shines upon our proceedings. It is trite to say to-day that we fought for freedom; that our sons and brothers fought for freedom in Flanders and France; but surely a primary consideration arising from that fact, which we all acknowledge with gratitude in the presence of the victory that we have achieved, is that having fought and won freedom in France and Flanders, we must take good care that it is not surrendered in Canada.
In my opinion we are, on this straight question and on this general principle of government, at the parting of the ways in Canada. We have been told ad nauseam, not only that our sons fought for freedom, but that they fought against autocracy. What is the weapon that autocracy used in Germany? I think I shall be right when I say that it was bureaucracy. Autocracy used bureaucracy as a weapon for the carrying out of its purposes of government. The consequence was that one of the prime causes of trouble in that country was that they had too much government, and as the case is in a number of other countries in Europe, to get rid of this, they had to reduce things to the state where there is very little government at all. We are not without our share of government in Canada. For a country of eight millions population we are a pretty well governed people. We have ten governments, ten prime ministers, ten parliaments, and ten sets of officials. I need not say that I do not intend this year to set up any active propagandism in favour of a change in the British North America Act, but the fact remains that under that Act we have a great deal of government, without establishing under any one of those governments any more bureaucracy than we can prevent. In my judgment, protectionism is, from this point of view, Kaiserism cut down. Protectionism and Kaiserism have a very close relation to one another. That was obviously so in Germany, because the Junkers were the backbone not only of the government, hut of protection and of the militaristic system in that country. Some one has said-and I think with a good deal of truth-that militarism itself is the spear head of protectionism. If that be so, then, as a peace-loving and democratic country, surely we

can get light from recent world events for examining this thing upon its merits from the root upwards. I think it can be demonstrated that there is a close political affinity between Kaiserism and protectionism. What was Kaiserism? It was from one point of view the magnification of the State into everything; it was the embodiment of despotic government. What is protectionism? It is an appeal to the State for assistance in doing one's own business. Protection arises because a certain class of persons come to the State and say: We would like a little help in the conduct of our business.
Well, what is the state, Mr. Speaker? I see the state sitting to your right and to your left to-day. This is all there is to the state. There is this peculiar thing about the state, that, divided as it has been from the time of Confederation up to the present into two halves, one-half of the state never has any confidence in the other half. I think the House will be in agreement with me upon that. As one half of the state never has any confidence in the other half, I may be illogical, but I do not think I am when I say that this should be a good reason for the people of this country being careful how they themselves bestow undue confidence upon the state.
I repeat, protectionists come to the state for assistance in their business, and what is the outgrowth of that? Is it to he supposed, human nature being what it is, that when other ranks of society see protectionists coming to the state and getting help for their business, that they should not think that a little help might be good for them, while it is going? That is exactly what happens, so we saw that in Germany, state socialism came to he the accompaniment of protectionism, and we are threatened in all protectionist countries .today with the same thing. I do not want to elaborate this very far as regards our own country, but it is a fact patent to the observation of every one of us that we are in the Government of Canada to-day absolutely inundated with commissions and boards and committees working under the Cabinet until I think one would be right in saying that we are threatened with a state of affairs in which politics will be the leading business of the country, and to get a Government job the highest ambition of the average ordinary citizen. Against that state of affairs I protest for this reason: Because it increases the cost of .Government by increasing the machinery of government. It increases the taxation of the people, and we are led to have done by Government a

number of things that under freedom people would do better for themselves.
From these general considerations I now pass a little more closely to the Budget. I cannot quite agree with my hon. friend from Marquette (-Mr. iCrerar)-and this is the only disagreement I shall have with him- in describing the Budget as a protectionist Budget. I think a fairer thing would be to define it-and I think history will so define it-as a Budget tending towards free trade. I am particularly grateful for the Budget. There was a time when I was charged with being the only free trade member of this House, but to-day, Sir, I am in the proud position of seeing a Government bring down into this House a Budget which proposes to lower tariffs. I have on my other hand an Opposition which says to the Government:	You are not lowering the
duties enough. I myself still occupy my old position, as between lower tariff on the one hand, and low tariff on the other, in believing in no tariff at all. ][DOT] repeat, I am proud to see that- the HTouse and the country is having its face at any rate turned in my direction. The tariff is coming down and therefore I would not like to use quite as strong language as my hon. friend from Marquette used about the Budget.
There are a good many things that can be said in favour of this Budget, even as compared with the amendment which has been moved by the Opposition. The Budget, has this advantage at least over the amendment: That it can be pointed to by its authors as having done something. It is embodied in resolutions, which, if they pass this House, will become the law of the land, and we must give a great deal of credit to people who- do things in preference to those who

for the moment they cannot do any better on the Opposition benches-only profess them. I do not want to be misunderstood on this point, and I do not want to go into ancient history; the times are too serious to spend much time in party quips and passes-I want to say again that the Opposition cannot do better in the circumstances in which they are placed. They can only profess to believe what is in the amendment, while the Government has the credit of having done what they have done. I think Western Canada will be grateful for so much.
I am perfectly sure that Western Canada will be grateful for another item which is not in the Budget. They will be very grateful that the Minister of Finance resisted very strong pressure which was brought to bear upon him to give certain
bounties in this Budget. The Government resisted what I know was very strong pressure, and they have not only done something in this Budget, but they have left some bad things undone. That may be news for the Opposition, but it is so, I think, and provably so as far as the Budget is concerned.
Then the Government have gone a very long way,-which shows the value of education in fiscal matters,-to embody in the statutes and law of this country the reciprocity agreement which they iwere not quite friendly to eight years ago; the reciprocity agreement is very largely embodied in the Budget proposals.
The Government also has imposed fairly steep direct taxation. Here the Budget has a very great advantage over the amendment offered from the other side, because I do not observe that direct taxation was mentioned in the amendment at all; not by specific proposals anyhow. I think the West will be grateful, not only for all these things, but, also, in a degree fitting the case, for such reduction of the tariff as there is. It is not satisfactory; it is not very abundant; but it is there.
As my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) pointed out yesterday, under the tariff war taxes the Minister of Finance raised $45,000,000, and he leaves $28,000,000 of that still to be got from the country. He relieves the country of the other $17,000,000. So the reduction of taxes is more apparent than real. We are not having a reduction of the tariff at all in this Budget as compared with the state of the tariff in pre-war times. Bather, we are having kept up in time of peace certain taxes which were impose^! in time of war, and which I think we might reasonably have expected to be relieved from now. If we are to regard this as a war year, as the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) indicated yesterday, there is something to be said for the point of view that it would have been better to leave the tariff alone this year; that would have been more logical. But, there is one over-powering reason for dealing with the tariff at this time, and that is to be found in the serious condition of the country. And from the point of view of the western organized farmers the tariff is not merely an instrument, but it is a vital and fundamental instrument in dealing with that serious condition of the country.
Now, my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) touched upon some very tender points yesterday as between himself and my hon. friend the member for

Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I do not intend to intervene in that quarrel any more than is necessary to clear up a few points in which I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration got quite the right view of the (question. He said, I think, that in his opinion the tariff was no issue in the 1917 election. I do not think that is a view that can be supported in its entirety. It is true that no specific proposals were before the country on the tariff from either side of politics. The winning of the war was the one all important issue in that election. But it is equally true that numbers of us from Western Canada could not have won our seats by the majorities we did, if indeed we could have won them at all, had we not asserted to our people, with all the sincerity that we were capable of, that we held the same views upon tariff matters that we had always held. So that it is not correct to say that the views of certain members of the Unionist party on tariff matters were not before the electors in the 1917 election. My hon. friend (Mr. Calder) went on to give us the reasons for his particular view of the duty of members of the Unionist party at this time. He said that there were certain grave problems before the country. Well, Mr. Speaker, we all know that. But what problems are they? They are no longer the problems of war; they are the problems of reconstruction. Every one of us who looked ahead at all knew that the war period would be succeeded by a reconstructive period, and these problems are problems of reconstruction. In 1917, as I have just pointed out, it was foreseen that we should come to this point in our history; and for (better or worse, right or wrong, my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar)-and a good many of us agree with him-believes that in the fiscal policy of the country is an instrument which, if wisely handled, will help us tremendously in dealing with the problems of reconstruction. That is the point where I think my hon. friend (Mr. Calder) was a little wrong in his view in blaming, so far as he did blame, the hon. member for Marquette. I did not apprehend at first that he intended to blame him at all. He laid down a perfectly sound doctrine in this matter when he said that in so serious a matter and at so serious a time every man must stand or fall by his own conscience; and I do not know that it was quite consistent with his having made that utterance that he immediately proceeded to take some rather ugly jabs at the conscience of my hon. friend from Mar-
quette. Now, in this connection, as explaining our position further, may I quote from my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, when he expressed the hope, as he did in his Budget speech, that by next fall, I think ho said, conditions will be so stabilized that ha can really safely begin to look into tariff matters. Well, one would be very sanguine in temperament to anticipate a great deal more stability next winter or the winter after that, even than one sees in the affairs of Canada at the present moment. I hope my hon. friend is right, but I am not going to enter into a competition in prophecy with him. What I am going to say is this: That it is not a government's business only to hope for stability; it. is a government's business to try to bring about conditions which tend to stability. Surely there is no contradicting that position. It is not enough to hope for stabilization. What would be thought of a doctor who was called to a delirious patient and was content with strapping him down in bed? You cannot produce stability alone by increasing the Northwest Mounted Police-that may be necessary; I believe it is necessary. You cannot produce stability alone by any proceedings of that kind. You must accompany your steps for preservation of law and order by measures to relieve public discontent so far as you can do it by financial, taxation, and trade propositions. If a patient is delirious a wise doctor straps him down in bed, but he does not for that reason neglect him in the matter of suitable food and medicine. The two things go together, if there is to be any chance of restoring the patient to health.
Now, what are the duties of reconstruction? We all agree that the first of them is to look after our soldiers. We shall only be able to look after our soldiers if we proceed as rapidly as we can to pay our debts as a nation. It is rather important both for the nation and for the individual that debts should be paid:	very important for the
debtor and very important for the other party himself. To pay our debts and look after our soldiers it is essential to increase the wealth of the nation; and to reconstruct the country it is equally necessary to relieve the burdens on the rank and file of our people. And I should add another principle of reconstruction: that it should be the duty of the Government to inculcate in civilization, thereby enriching it, a spirit of service, of sacrifice, and of hard work, and so give the people the luxury of approach- .* ing in some degree the moral grandeur of the half million of men who crossed the

sea, willing to give everything for the glory and honour of their country and the freedom of civilization and mankind.
Now, I am afraid that I have to say that the Budget falls short of what it should have measured up to along these lines. I have been reminded in private that 1 have said in this House and elsewhere that it took some nineteen years to build up the free trade edifice in Britain, or rather to pull down the tariff edifice. That is quite true. But that statement does not meet my objection that we are not doing enough in this Budget along the lines I have advocated. This will be apparent if the House will permit me to read a few words from a speech which Sir Robert Peel delivered on March 11, 1842, and to tell the House what he did in the way of fiscal proposals in that year, which was four years before the repeal of the Corn Laws. Speaking on that occasion, Sir Robert Peel laid down principles which ought to be a great guide for all time, to finance ministers, in periods of great financial difficulty in any country. He said:
In great financial difficulties the first step towards improvement is to look those difficulties boldly in the face. This is true of individuals ; it is also true of nations.
To look those difficulties boldly in the face-I am not sure that my hon. friend the Finance Minister of this country has done so in the sense of the language of Sir Robert Peel, who went on to make this statement -and the House will notice he expected the unanimous consent of the House of Commons to the proposition:
I apprehend therefore, that with almost universal acquiescence I may abandon the thought of supplying the deficiency by the miserable device of fresh loans.
Mr. Speaker, that is very strong language, and I commend it to the careful attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. What did Sir Robert Peel do in 1842? But here our present Government is on very much stronger ground. What Sir Robert Peel did in 1842 was to introduce direct taxation in the shape of an income tax for the first time. In that connection let me say that there was a great deal of political wisdom in what was suggested to this House in what some regard as the somewhat puzzling speech of the hon. the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton). He claimed, and claimed, I think, rightly, for this Government that in the income tax which it has presented to this House it had laid the most solid foundation for either party in this country to pursue fiscal reforms in the future along the proper line -the line of lower tariff. But, Sir Robert Peel did not stop with introducing the income tax. In the first budget that Sir Robert Peel introduced into Great Britain in 1842, he practically put all raw materials on the free list. He left on some duties but he left no duty of more than five per cent on any raw material whatsoever. On partially manufactured articles he left no duty of over 12 per cent and on wholly manufactured goods he left no duty exceeding 20 per cent. Out of 1,200 articles contained in the tariff schedules of Britain before that budget, he reduced or abolished the taxation on 750 and he did it in so far as history records without any tariff commission running all over the country. He was determined upon a great reform, he saw that the country needed it, that no further delay could toe brooked in the matter, and that is the way in which he tackled it.
Having regard to this historical record. I purposed, if the rules of the House had allowed, introducing a sub-amendment which would have gone a little farther than either the proposals of the Government or the proposals of the Opposition as I understand them. Might I be permitted to say, Sir, that a rule that does not allow a subamendment appears to me to be an absurd anomaly and I trust that one of these days, either yourself, or some other Speaker of the House, will see that that rule is abolished. It seems an absurd anomaly that there has never been since Confederation in contemplation the possibility of three groups in this House or the possibility of expressing three different opinions upon the Budget. I purposed if I had been allowed, asking the House to affirm that:
Inasmuch as any scheme of tariff reduction is faulty and illogical which is not calculated to stimulate equally all the industries of our country, so necessary to reconstruction, therefore be it resolved,
1st. That the removal of the duties from all foodstuffs .and from the implements used in their production should be accompanied by the abolition of duties on iron and steel the raw materials of these implements and many other manufactures.
2nd. That the abolition of the duties on boots, shoes and articles of cotton and woollen clothing should be accompanied by the removal of duties on raw materials entering into the production of these articles.
3rd. That all duties should be removed from coal, which is so large a factor in the producing power of our factories and the comfort of our homes.
4th. That debt should be reduced and further borrowing as much as possible avoided by the imposition of increased income tax and

super-tax, a federal succession or inheritance tax and a tax on land values.
I think the House will agree that such an amendment as this would have been a procedure approximating much more closely to the first step taken by Sir Robert Peel along the same line in England and would have done more to meet the western point of view than either the Budget proposals or the proposal contained in the amendment. But as there is a little lack of heroism on the part of both the old parties in -Canada, and as there is, in my view, an imperfection in the rules of the House, one has to look carefully at the proposals of the Government on the one hand, and the amendment before the House on the other hand, to see what course one shall take after he has read his still-born sub-amendment.
My fault with the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) is that it requires a little too much interpretation. It needs to be interpreted. I agree with very much of it; if I am allowed to interpret it and supplement it, I think I should agree with it all, but, of course, it would not be the same amendment. The part of it which calls for free food, I agree with absolutely. Mr. Speaker, there is no excuse in Canada for anybody being short of plenty to eat three times a day. With our sparse population, our abundant territory and great wealth, there is no excuse in Canada for any tax whatsoever upon food. I want to put that idea forward and to state it so emphatically as to carry my profound convictions in the truth of what I am saying to both sides of this House and, through both sides of this House, to the country. I am convinced, furthermore, that in what I am stating I have the support of the large majority of the people of the country, men, women and children.
The cost of living in its relation to food should be at the -minimum in Canada. I know there are opposite views expressed. No less an authority than the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) to whom I always want to pay the utmost attention, expressed a doubt whether the cost of living would be reduced by the removal of duties on food. I have heard the same question put myself in committee, in caucus, and in private conversation. Well, I think it would be reduced and I will tell the House why in a moment. But if it would not be reduced because there is no food to come in, which is the further assertion always made in accordance with this argument, if there is no food to come into the

country; if we could not get any food into the country at the present moment, and for that reason the taking of the tariff off food *would not reduce the cost, then
4 p.m. all I have to say is that reduction is well worth trying anyhow because if the tariff has kept nothing out it is a very unnecessary and useless piece of national equipment. The tariff, if it has kept nothing out, is- not doing any good along that line but it would be worth while trying for a Government that was not altogether heroic just to see what would happen. I contend that there is no scarcity of food in Canada. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister on the occasion to which I refer, said that in the various countries in which he had been travelling the cost of living was as high as it is in Canada. I have no doubt as to the accuracy of his observation in the hotels in which he dined, but some returned soldiers, who observed the buying of bacon by the pound in the old country-I am sure my right hon. friend had not much time to buy bacon by the pound-assert, and assert quite confidently, the exact contrary, and say that you can buy bacon cheaper in England to<lay than you can buy it in Canada by the pound.
If that is so, then it is a serious reflection upon our economic system. It is the more serious when I tell the House that according to figures in the last edition of the Canadian Year Book, for eight millions of people in Canada there are twice as many live pigs to-day as there are in Great Britain amongst forty .millions of people. Now, if there are only half the number of live pigs for forty millions of people in England that there are in Canada for eight millions of people it is something of a miracle that the price of bacon is kept as low in England as it is. How is it kept as low, or brought lower? By the simple fact that Britain brings it in; Britain brings bacon across the seas to her shores freely-she brings food in. The fact of the matter is that the tariff on foodstuffs in this country does little or no good to the producer. It does a great deal of harm to the consumer, and it builds up the fortunes of the middlemen-that is what the tariff does on foodstuffs in this country. I have cited a simple figure in regard to live pork. Now let me give the House the figure in regard to cattle. There are, or were when the figures were collected last for the Canadian Year Book seven and a half million head of cattle in Great Britain with forty millions of people; there were six and a half million head at the same date in Canada with eight millions of

people. Why should food he scarce in Canada? Six and a half millions of cattle as against seven and a half millions in Britain, and eight millions of people as compared with forty millions; and twice as many pigs in Canada for eight millions of people! There is only one answer: The food is being held from the people for exorbitant prices and the building up, beyond the dreams of avarice, of the fortunes of the middlemen.
With the item in the amendment of the Opposition which calls for free food I am in hearty agreement; and coming as I do from the West I need scarcely add that I am in hearty agreement with free implements for the production of that food.
But now I come to the clause in the amendment which needs interpretation. There is a clause in that amendment which calls for " free necessities of life." If it had stopped there it still would have needed interpretation to the extent of defining what you mean by " a necessity of life." Personally, I think coal is a necessity of life in a country where you have eight months of winter and the thermometer going sometimes to sixty degrees below zero. I think a good case can be made out in the argument that coal is a necessity of life. I do not think it would make much difference to a man whether he perishes for want of coal, or starves to death for want of food; I am not sure which I should choose if the dread alternative were offered to me. I think coal is a necessity of life, and I wonder if my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition so interprets the amendment. Perhaps it is not fair to aSk him to interpret the amendment of 'the hon. member for Bromer (Mr. McMaster). Whether he will interpret it or not, I am pretty sure it required an older head than the member for Brome to draw the amendment in that 'beautifully vague fashion; I rather suspect that vague clause in the amendment was drawn by the leader of the Opposition. Well, I gather from his attitude now that he disavows the paternity of it, but he won't interpret it to me. Then he will have to try and prove to me when he speaks at a later stage, and he certainly will have to try 'and prove to this country when he comes into power, that coal is not a necessity of life, because he is pledged by this amendment to free " the necessities of life," and I contend, not being a lawyer, that a good case can be made out for calling coal " a necessity of life." In any case, I believe in free coal, and I think there is a splendid argument
to be advanced not only for abundant food for people who live in a hard and trying climate like Canada, not only for free food, but also for free fuel-free fuel for homes, and free fuel to enable our manufacturers to contend in the tremendous competition of the coming years in the industries of the country.
Then I believe in boots and shoes, and woollen and cotton clothing being necessities of life. Apart altogether from the decencies of life, the climate demands that we wear clothes in Canada for a great part of the year. They are necessities of life; so are boots and shoes; and I have yet to meet a Canadian who can give me a good reason why, at this moment, boots and shoes are absolutely free on the tariff of the United States, and have been carrying a duty of thirty and thirty-five per cent in this country. There is nothing in the price of hides to account for it at the present moment, because the western farmer at the present time is practically giving his hides away. Being of benevolent disposition, I do not suppose he would mind that very much if the consumers got the benefit; but he is very decidedly up in arms when he sees the tremendous price that goes on to the hide between the time it leaves him, for little or nothing, and reaches the wearer of the boots.
While interpreting it in this way, the amendment does not begin to look so bad, always including the free coal and the free boots and shoes. Now I get on to more difficult ground when I read into the clause about the necessities of life, free iron and steel. Iron and steel are articles very much used in the making of railways. In a country of the size of Canada we talk half our time in Parliament about the building of railroads, and we have a tremendous agitation to get railroads built in this country. It is frequently argued that protection is more necessary in a young country than in an old country from the point of view of iron and steel. Mr. Speaker, I think that protection is a much greater curse in a young country than in an old one, because an old country, especially of small size, is always gridironed with railways; but where you are building railroads by the thousands of miles, as you are in Canada, at first sight it would not seem to expedite the business to make iron and steel dear. But that is one of the wonderful contradictions of protection, that a good way to build railroads is to have dear iron and steel. I submit the opposite to that contention, and I hold that would

be at least worth thinking over even by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Cheap iron and steel would help not only the building of railroads but the easier production of mining, of agricultural and otheT classes of machinery, which are used in the productive industries which constitute so much of the industries of a young people like the people of Canada. Indeed, these are the very .basic needs of a young country. If I wanted to argue this question further I should isay that in Nova Scotia, where there is a large iron and steel industry, it will be safe to prophesy that if you had free trade to-morrow, Nova Scotia would benefit more in the development of her coal and iron industries by the amount of shipping that would ply to and from her shores than by being engaged in the production and selling of the iron and steel, and killing her shipping.
I should like to put again on Hansard some figures that I think I quoted some years ago, to show that the idea that protection is needed to build up the industries of a country finds very little support in the history of the greatest commercial nation for all time, at least for her size. In the year 1800 the value of the exports of British produce, which of course were manufactured products, was thirty-nine and a half millions sterling. In the year 1830, after the first thirty years of the nineteenth century, when protection was in full sway in Great Britain, the figure of thirty-nine and a half millions of exported produce actually fell to thirty-seven millions- -£37,000,000 as against £39,500,000 as a result of the first thirty years of the 19th century manufacturing under protection. In the year 1842, after twelve more years, the figure had grown by £10,000,000 a year to £50,000,000. But railroads began to be built in Great Britain at that time and accounted amply for the rise to £50,000,000. The bald fact, however, is this, that between 1800 and 1842 the manufactured exports of Great Britain under the last forty-two years of protection rose from £39,500.000 to only £50,000,000. In the year 1878, when thirty-six	more years	had passed
over the history of Great [Britain, under a free trade policy her exported manufactured goods had risen from £50,000,000 to £218,000,000 per year; in the last twelve years of protection it showed only a £10,000,000 advance. It rose during thirty-six years of free trade to £218,000,000, and by the year 1910 that figure had risen to £344,000,000, which constituted a record export for all nations and all tariffs-a record

export held and made under free trade. I do not think if one were to read figures from now until bed-time that it would be possible to controvert the obvious inference to be drawn from these figures, that Great Britain until she had free trade never really had manufactures worth speaking of.
I not only want to interpret the amendment, but I want to be allowed to supplement it. And the point at which it needs supplementing is one that puts considerable suspicion in one's mind as to certain things that do not appear in the amendment at all. I have already said that I think the Budget has a great advantage over the amendment of the Opposition in that it imposes very substantial direct taxation. So far as the amendment of the Opposition goes, it is blank upon this subject. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. iMcMaster) indeed told the Minister of Finance that he should stop borrowing. IBut how can he stop borrowing and at the same time lower the tariff if he is not shown some other method of raising the revenue? I want to say quite candidly that I associate myself fully with my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) in his opinion that the direct taxation proposed by the Budget, though a tremendous advance on anything that Canada has ever dreamed of before, is not sufficient for the times we are passing through, and is not sufficient to carry out that principle that I laid down when I said that it is the duty of the Finance Minister by taxation to teach that economy which he preaches, and to teach the far more valuable lesson that this war will have been lost in moral value upon our civilian population unless they are taught to approach somewhat to the sacrifices that were made by those who for four years bled and suffered and died for us.
I think my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) mentioned yesterday comparative figures as between Canada and Great Britain in regard to income tax. I now quote only figures of two incomes. And I approach this subject with considerable diffidence because I came from the Old Country and I have no right to set standards for Canadians, ibut I would fain have them set standards for themselves, because Canada's sons suffered just as Great Britain's sons suffered, Canada's sons fought just as Great Britain's sons fought, and I do not believe that the fathers and the mothers of Canada are one whit less willing to suffer in their pockets than are the fathers and mothers df Great Britain. In Great Britain a $10,000 income to-day pays an income tax of $2,775, and in Canada it

pays $590. There is a great disparity between those two figures, Mr. Speaker. A $20,000 income in "Canada pays $1,990, while in Great Britain it pays $5,775. As I say,
I have' no right to enforce this point any more than the figures do, but I should like to ask both sides of this House whether it is not our hounden duty as a Parliament to give our people a chance of coming a little nearer to the British standards in this matter.
We are asked: How are you going to raise revenue if you abolish tariffs? In the sub-amendment which I would have moved if the rules of the House would have allowed . me I intended to ask the Minister of Finance to impose a federal succession duty; and in this connection I do not compare this country with Great Britain, where they have very large duties, but with Australia, who also suffered with us in the battlefields. It is estimated by our chief statistician that the total wealth of Aus-ralia is $8,000,000,000; Canada's wealth is $19,000,000,000-a startling difference. It almost appears to me sometimes. Sir, as if this country were the happy hunting ground of capital, and I believe we have been taught such a lesson by this war that our people are getting to know too much to allow that to go on. Australia raised last year by a federal succession duty $5,000,000; we raised nothing. By provincial succession duties Australia raised $4,500,000, and we raised about the same. That is to say, if we had taxed ourselves by way of succession duty as heavily as Australia is doing, instead of $4,500,000 of provincial succession duties only we should have been taxed under this head for federal and provincial purposes $25,000,000. And I point this out to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance with every desire to help him towards his next Budget as a line along $20,000,000 that is going abegging.
In the debate of 1915-because in every year of the war before the formation of Union Government in 1917 we actually had no land tax,-I laid down the doctrine which I am trying to inculcate to-day in my humble manner; in 1915 I pointed out that the year before Australia had raised $13,500,000 by land tax; in 1915 we had not raised a cent. We have much better land and more of it than in Australia, and we have a larger population, have large amounts of land, as my hon. friend for Marquette so well pointed out yesterday, held in Western Canada by speculators, having its value augmented tremendously by the efforts of those who hold land

in the neighbourhood and live on it. And that ought, in the strenuous and terrible times succeeding this war, to be made the source of Federal revenue for the purposes of looking after our soldiers, clearing our debt, and relieving our people of the tremendous burden they are bearing in the matter of the common necessities of life.
But we are told: You will frighten capital away from the country; you will not be able to borrow any more money. In my opinion that would not be a bad job for Canada. I agree absolutely with the hon. member for Brome (Mr; McMaster) when he says: Stop borrowing. It is well at this point to remember what we do economically when we borrow. When we borrow money, either from the United States or from the old country, what we do is to give an enormous and immediate stimulus to the industries of the country from which we borrow, because I need not tell this intelligent House that what we borrow comes in, not in the shape of money, but in the shape of goods. When we borrow from another country, we get simply a cheque which is changed into exchange notes and becomes a purchasing agent for the goods of the country from which we borrow. And one of the reasons why I doubt very much the wisdom of those economists who tell us that we must be a borrowing country in Canada, is that when we borrow, like it or not like it, the economic truth is that we stimulate not, in the first instance, our own industries, but those of the country from which we borrow.
I have heard a great deal of extravagant praise given to the Victory Loans, and I understand we are to have another domestic loan floated. It is as well for us to understand economically what a domestic loan is, how it operates. These loans are bought and owned, necessarily, mostly by the wealthy people of the country, because you do not get them unless you have the money to pay for them. They are owned free of taxation; they are bought by the wealthy who have made millions in the war; and the interest upon them will, we have been assured by the Minister of Finance, be extended over a large number of future years upon the devoted heads of the rank and file of the people of this country, if you continue to raise your revenue by a tariff. Therefore, the loans being owned by the wealthy, the interest will be	paid,	first by	every returned
soldier and his wife and family upon the clothes which he wears and the boots and

socks which his family wear; second, by the ranks of labour; third, by the farmers; and fourth, by the general consuming public of the country. Under those conditions, I have no hesitation in saying that I am not a five and-a-half per cent patriot myself. There is no patriotism in those loans, and while that is a very strong statement to make, many that have bought them say: We do not profess to be patriots in buying upon the credit of the Dominion of Canada at five and-a-half per cent; you could not get a better financial investment upon the surface of the world. That is how I view these loans, and that is why I emphatically endorse the advice of the hon. member for Brome when he says: Stop borrowing. Nineteen billions of dollars of a total wealth is Canada's wealth as compared with eight billions of dollars in Australia, and I am to be asked: Where shall be get the revenue ? When we floated our last loan, the people of Canada subscribed $600,000,000 in three weeks. If we had taxed that wealth properly we would have taken $300,000,000 of that somehow or another, and we would never had to pay interest or pay back capital, and things would have been squared with the profiteers if we had done that. That is where we should get the money. But, a finance minister who cannot get money to carry on the business of a small country with a small population like this, with nineteen billion dollars of wealth rolling around, wants some assistance in the running of his business. I emphasize this point, because I remember well that in the last election-and this I want to put strongly to the Government-the phrase was used upon every platform: We are behind the boys in France and Flanders to the last man and the last dollar. I have given the Government all the support in my power and all the credit that is coming to them, because they put sufficient emphasis on the man. Now I want the emphasis on the money. I am logical; I am patriotic, and I believe the people of Canada will demand that that shall be done, because I am certain that the people of Canada in their innermost natures are as great-hearted and as good people as are to be found anywhere on the face of this earth. We were told at the last election, as we have been told on innumerable platforms since the beginning of the war, that after the war things were not to be the same; that nothing was to be the sartie-nothing excepting tariffs and the millions of the profiteers. That is surely not our doctrine.
I think the minister should have gone further along this line of taxation. 
The supreme condemnation of tariff lies in this, that while it draws most of the taxes of the country from the poor, it at the same time, imposes upon the poor the heaviest burden of living, while it builds up the fortunes of the rich and fails to tax the rich even as much as the poor in the numerous cases where the poor have larger families than the rich.
We have been talking and are hearing a great deal about the unrest and the discontent there are in the country. It is these conditions that the Government has the power to relieve that I want to impress upon them. It is these considerations that are burning themselves into the hearts and minds of our people, that are stirring up the discontent. Society was stirred to its foundations by this war, and it is to-day stirred to its foundations by the consideration that the cost of living is bringing the actual pinch to make ends meet into 75 to 80 per cent of our homes, while the other 20 per cent are living in luxury, which Is flaunted everywhere. Society has been compared to a stream with two banks, and I try to visualise it as such to-day. On the one bank there are few inhabitants, comparatively, walking amidst flowers, riding in automobiles, dressed in the finest, occupying boxes at the theatres, having joy rides at home and pleasure trips abroad, lavishing in plenty beyond the description of words-on the other bank there is the great mass of the returned soldiers, the labouring people and the farmers getting up at early dawn and working until bedtime, and between the two banks there floats this sullen stream of discontent. On both banks every individual can say with the utmost truth: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither." It is a terrible thing that in a country where there should be plenty there should be such disparity of fortune, and every right thinking man, whether he be in private life or in a public position, will reflect with greatest pleasure when he comes, as we have been reminded by recent events we shall all too soon come, to the end of life, on any efforts he has made, whether as an individual or as a legislator, to bridge that stream of discontent by bringing about, so far as law can do so, a greater equality of fortune amongst all the masses of our people.
We have been told more than once in this debate that free trade versus protection is an old controversy. Well, there are older controversies than that in the world-that of original sin, for instance. That is much

older, and I do not know that anybody wants to put up with sin for all that; we want to get rid of it. The tariff is old enough. It is so old that it is losing caste to-day among people who formerly thought a great deal of it. A very genial and good friend of mine among the members of this House was good enough to put a letter in my box the other day expressing the hope that I would define free trade. I am very glad to oblige him, if the House will permit me. Free trade is the assertion of the right of every man and every nation to buy in the cheapest and sell in the dearest market without the law intervening to help any given set of producers. That looks a very sensible and decent thing. It is a right we all assert for ourselves when the Government leaves us alone. We all like to buy in the cheapest and to sell in the dearest market.
I have already submitted in the course of my remarks this afternoon a definition, or an illustration, of protection. Why, the very word protection is beginning to smell, especially in the light of the events of this war. What grown man should want protection anyhow? We have discarded the need of it on our western farms; we do not ask for it. We are all British through and through out there, and all we ask is a fair field and no favour, which is an old British proverb. Our sons and brothers in the trenches did not want protection; it was the fellows they went up against that needed protection. And yet, hon. gentlemen in this House for whom I have very great respect stand up and ask for protection, but I am glad they do so apologetically. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition the other day grieved me when he said: "I am a protectionist." But then he apologized. "Not a very large one," he said. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) said that he also was a protectionist, but not a very large one. The leader of the Opposition is in favour of protection, just a little bit in Nova Scotia for iron and steel and coal. I do not know what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wants protected. My hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) closed his speech last night by saying "I a*m a protectionist." Hie has to be at the present moment, because he has just had a little piece shaved off, and I should not wonder if he became one of my chief apostles now for shaving the other fellow. That is the way it is bound to work, and no one knows it better than the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert
Ames). In the reciprocity debate eight years ago, in a speech I very well remember, he described wheat as the keystone of the protectionist arch, and he said if wheat was taken away the whole arch would fall. I hope he was a good prophet, and I hope I shall be there to see the arch tumble.
Protection needs to be apologized for today. It was beaten in argument long ago, and on this continent. May I give to the House a brief exposure of protection, and a splendid motto for re-construction, from that great literary philosopher, Ralph Waldo Emerson. They have not all been protectionists in America. The best prose writer that country ever produced had this to say:
The way to mend the had world is to create the right world, Here is a low political economy plotting to cut the throat of foreign competition and establish our own; excluding others, by force, or making wtar on them-
He knew the connection between protection and militarism.
-or by cunning tariffs giving preference to worse wares of ours. But the real and lasting victories are those of peace and not of war. The way to conquer the foreign artisan is, not to kill him, but to beat his work.
There is a fine moral tonic both for men and for Governments facing reconstruction, and here I would even be so venturesome as to try and improve upon the mottp which the Minister of Finance has thrown out to this nation. He said: " Produce and save." I would say, " Work and trade." If you work hard enough you will not spend too much, and if you trade hard enough you have to produce stuff to trade with. Trade is before production. No one is going to produce things unless he can dispose of them. " Work and trade" would be the motto I would recommend to this country during reconstruction.
The argument for free trade was won long ago by words, but in this war, Mr. Speaker, I claim that it has been won to a world demonstration by events. How have fiscal policies stood the test of the greatest war the world ever saw? Great Britain raised seven million men to fight by sea and land But for her navy not an American soldier could have landed in Europe. We have the high testimony of a man who does not waste words, General Foch, who says that in the last grim conflict it was the hammer blows of the British army that brought about the German debacle. Having done all that on land and sea in the early stages of the war, she financed herself, financed the Allies, and the outlying portions of the

Empire, and to-day she is the only belligerent country in Europe that is solvent. I hate to say anything that seems to reflect upon France, but facts must be stated, and it is a fact that France's notes would not run in the United States at this moment if they were not backed by the little free trade island of Great Britain. That is the record of how free trade stood the strain of the greatest war in history. We did our share in that war.
I have paid my tribute before to the men composing this Government who carried our part in the war to a successful conclusion, and I want to pay my tribute now onoe more to the Prime Minister of this country who shares with General Botha the proud distinction of being the only two Prime Ministers who have occupied that position from the beginning to the end of the war. That credit is coming to the Prime Minister of Canada. Credit is also coming to him for the very great patience and effort by which he formed Union Government, without which one questions whether the war would have been carried on as we, on this side of the House at least, wished it to be carried on.
Might I appeal to the party with whom I have been associated for two years to keep an open mind upon this question of freedom? We fought for freedom. Let us have freedom in Canada. I wish to end on this point as I began-I am not wedded to any special method of fiscal reform, but a great service will be done for the freedom of the world, a tremendous service will be done for the building up of this Empire, and for the development of Canada to greater glories along the financial and economic line than she has ever dreamt of, when the policy of British preference first enunciated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is extended further until we have absolute free trade between the Mother Country and this great Dominion. Why should we not have it? Will Canada lose anything by being linked up to the greatest commercial entity of all times? Lose! She will gain infinitely,. Great Britain is not only a tremendous market for the commodities which we have to sell, but she is the emporium for the world's commerce. Why should we not be linked up to her absolutely freely commercially.
When that intrepid man from Australia, Hawker, with his equally intrepid companion attempted his transatlantic flight amid the breathless excitement and expectation and hopes and sympathies of a world

looking on, he could not do it from his own home in the southern seas. He had to come not far off from the shores of Canada to attempt his flight. Was there not in that an inspiration for us? Was there not a lesson for us in the fact? It is from the shores of Canada that this linking up process must be effected-a condition which will be one of the greatest compensations of the war. From these shores must come this linking up of all who speak the English language and understand and appreciate British institutions. It is from Canada, I reiterate, that all the linking up must originate. The little islands in the North sea held their hands out to us at the beginning of the war and they were readily and tightly clasped and held until together we carried the war to a successful conclusion. They are held out to us now again. We have a free market there for our goods. Five short days compass the journey between the two countries, and Canada's future greatness would receive a most tremendous impetus from this course. Our blood was mixed forever in union on the battlefields of Europe. We are united politically, and a rich blessing of material good, and the future peace and glory not only of the Empire but of the world, await the party or the man who will unite us to Britain commercially.

bring my mind to believe that the actual day of conflict is over. One thing I am sure of, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the day of trouble and of difficulty is not over. One thing I am fully satisfied of is that apart from the single question of the loss of life which, I hope, will not be continued, as great troubles, as great difficulties and as serious problems confront us as confronted us during the last four years. During the period of the war this country as a whole-as a whole, I say-was united. We were agreed as a whole upon the great issue before us. Can anybody to-day, in his sane moments, assert that 5 p.m. this country is united on almost any single question that could be presented before a public audience? It is not simply a difference of opinion on minor or superficial matters, but the people are at variance on questions which, in my. judgment, are as vital to the well-lbeing of Canada and as essential to the prosperity and suoeess of this nation as were the issues before this country during the war. We are in just as serious a situation to-day as we were four years ago. I have recently crossed this continent and I know something of the spirit which prevails in the western provinces. The hon. gentleman from Red Deer made ia very earnest and eloquent plea for the perpetuation of liberty in this country and in this House. Does my hon. friend not know that on this very day and for the last three or four weeks, there have been thousands and thousands of men and women in the four western provinces who have been fighting for liberty just as seriously and just as earnestly as they ever did during the four years of the war? We are not at peace. Were I the rankest free trader west of Winnipeg-were I the rankest free trader in Canada; moreover, were I a member of this Cabinet-I would think hard and long before I would take any step that even- appeared to strike a blow at the Government of Canada. Hon. members on the other side of the House may smile at that.
Let me say that it is not simply striking a blow at Union Government. Men in this House do not know the facte. I have read in- history that while Rome was burning, Nero fiddled. There is almost -a counterpart of that situation at this day. It is not simply striking a blow at the Union Government; the situation to-day in the western country means -striking a blow at government. Make no mistake about th-at. Let no one be so blinded by partisanship as not to realize that it is not any one Government

that is assailed to-day. It is not Union Government and a Conservative Government is not now in the province of Manitoba. The aim is to strike a blow at government-all governments-and, therefore, I say with all -modesty and seriousness that it is a terribly serious thing for any minister of the Crown at this stage of the game to even appear to strike a blow at, or to embarrass, the Government of Canada.
What is the situation? I am no alarmist. I am accustomed to be somewhat moderate and calm but a man must open his eyes to-day to the facts and acknowledge the truth. I said a moment ago that there were men and women in- the provinces of the West who were literally and actually sacrificing and fighting to-day for liberty. Let me make that statement stronger. Let me tell the hon. member for Marquette and the hon. member for Red Deer and every other man in this House who regards the tariff as the supreme question that they are mistaken. West of the Great Lakes the one great thought running through the minds of men and women is this: Shall the Union Jack float over our cities or the red rag of revolution?
References have been made, Sir, by the eloquent gentlemen who have spoken-references are frequently made-to the labour men, and to the returned soldier. That reference -has a popular ring; it is a fine appeal to the gallery. It is a splendid slogan to use, this appeal to the labour men and to our returned soldiers, as though Parliament were opposed in any way to the rights of the former and were not desirous of doing justice to the latter. Does this House not know-it surely must know -that this is not a labour strike? If any hon. gentleman does not know it, I take the responsibility of telling him-this is not, strictly -speaking, a labour strike. I grant you it has the appearance of it, and I do not propose at the present moment to enter into any lengthened discussion of the labour situation-this is not the time for it. But I want to give the House two or three reasons for the assertion I have made. The materialistic philosophy of the nineteenth century gave birth to two great heresies: one of them, Sir, was. the heresy of the superman, and the other was the heresy of the under man. The heresy ol the superman had its culmination in Prussian militarism, and was overthrown upon the battlefields of Europe; the heresy of the under man has not yet been overthrown. Let no one think for a moment, as -has been intimated, that the Bolsheviki terror is an aftermath of the war. It is

nothing of the kind. It was born long before the war. It was what I have termed the heresy of the under man. It was known in France first by the name of Syndicalism. It was known in Russia by the name of Bolshevism. It was known in the United States first by the name ol I.W.W-ism. It is known in Australia, in Great Britain, and in Canada, by the name of "One Big Unionism." It is the same thing, gentlemen; it is the same thing in different forms. It has flourished in England during the war. It bids fair to enter upon a career that can scarcely be outlined. You know its dominancy to-day in Australia. It has had one fight already on this continent, m the city of Seattle, and was vanquished. The second conflict on the continent of America is in progress to-day in the city of Winnipeg. Do not be misled by the assertion that this is a labour strike.
That brings me, Sir, to another point. "One Big Unionism" has been seeking for a long time to secure the co-operation not only of labour but also of the returned soldier. Shall I pause a moment and repeat that "One Big Unionism" has been moving heaven and earth to secure the sympathy and the co-operation of our returned soldiers. To some extent, in some cases, I grant you they have succeeded. A few have yielded to the courtship and have given their sympathy and support to it, perhaps not knowing fully what they were doing -yet they have done so. But let me say that the great majority of the returned men of the Canadian West are true to the principles for which my eloquent friend (Mr. Michael Clark) made such a powerful plea -the principles of liberty. They will not be dominated in Canada by the underman, as they refused to be dominated in Europe by the superman. That is -where the great struggle of this country is to-day concentrated : as to who shall obtain control of the great forces known as the labour element.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are other things I would like to say, but shall not proceed further than to admit that we are to blame, a great deal to blame, for the labour unrest in Canada to-day. That is owing in part to two things. Let me say to you that the labouring men of this country have a very strong and pronounced objection to what are known in Canada as our land policies, both Dominion and provincial. We have made some great blunders in the past with regard to our public lands. The records placed on the table of the House the other day show that nearly thirty-two million.
acres of public lands have been given to corporations, and let .me say in passing that nearly twenty-nine million acres of those were given between the years 1890 and 1911. In the parting with those lands is to be found one cause of unrest. Another cause lies in the fact that the great employers of labour in Canada have not dealt justly with the labouring men. I do not hesitate to say that because I believe it to be true. They have a feeling that until they used the weapon of compulsion they were exploited. They believed, rightly or wrongly, that they have not received a square deal in the operation of the great industries of the country. I shall not go further into that question except to say that from my own observation and study of this question there is only one solution. There is, I believe, one solution, but it is not along the lines suggested by my horn, friend (Mr. Cockshutt) last night, nor along the lines suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Michael Clark) this afternoon. You could build a tariff fence around this Dominion eight rails high, with a rider on top of that again, and it would not solve the existing industrial problem. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) could tear down that tariff fence, level it to the ground and burn every rail, and still the difficulty and the unrest would remain. That would not help the situation. -It might satisfy him for a while, but it would not satisfy the great labour element of the country. What is the solution? It is simply this: A practical, sympathetic, and actual business co-operation with the employee. That, gentlemen, is the solution, in the judgment of many men to-day, of the great labour unrest which prevails in Canada. We have that industrial problem before us. The strike is not, I believe, in the last analysis, a real labour trouble; it is the subtle attempt to exercise influence and power, with the design of destroying government-all governments, any government. It is that power which is seeking to-day the co-operation of the labour forces of this country, and which, to some extent, appears to be succeeding.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if that be so, let us seriously consider whether or not it is our business to discuss hour after hour superficial questions, or whether we should not seriously and assiduously set ourselves to the task of really attempting to solve the great issue and the great difficulty which is confronting this country to-day. You read your papers morning after morning, and you note what is going on in that western country, and I want to say to this House

that this is no time for the discussion ot questions which are not involved distinctly in the programme of Union Government as it was settled by the country in December, 1917.
Reference was made last night by the hon. gentleman from Maisonneuve to a visit to this House by Mr. Samuel Gompers. I thought he rather attempted to make light of that visit, to ridicule it. Perhaps not so, but that was the impression upon my mind. For my part, I am delighted that we had the opportunity of hearing and recognizing such a champion of labour as Mr. Samuel Gompers. If there is one man on this North American continent, especially in the United States, that the I.W.W. and other revolutionaries are attacking from every angle it is Samuel Gompers.

My hon. friend is mistaken. I never alluded to the visit of Mr. Gompers. I was here and welcomed him and was proud to have him the guest of Canada. I alluded to the telegram sent by the Minister of Labour to Mr. Gompers.
I am glad to have that explanation.
I am a great admirer of Mr. Gompers.
I am glad to know that my hon. friend did not exactly mean what he appeared to say.

The hon. gentleman
ought to accept my explanation. If he was not here last night be might read Hansard.
