I shall make another attempt, Sir. The hon. gentleman made reference to a man whom he termed the leader of this movement in the city of Winnipeg, and wanted to know who he was. Is that right? Now, I shall tell him. Until a couple of years ago the gentleman was the pastor of a church of one of the larger Protestant denominations in the province of Manitoba. That relation was severed. Since then he has been nominally the spiritual guide of the revolutionary party, and of the labour party also, in the city of Winnipeg. And I have one other item of information to give the hon. member which may not be so com-

forting-this same gentleman was the recognized leader of the anti-conseriptionist party in the city of Winnipeg during the last election.
Now I come, Sir, to what I may call personal reasons why I intend to vote against the amendment. The hon. gentleman from Marquette told us yesterday that he was going to vote against the Government because of principle. I do not claim to have principles any better than those of my hon. friend. But I am an older man, and perhaps my convictions are a bit deeper in consequence. The war has come to him, I presume, as to many another man as a citizen of Canada. But, Sir, the iron has pierced my soul-time can never heal the wound. What I have said with regard to myself can be said with regard to many a man in this iHtause. To many of us, as to thousands more in this Dominion, home and the family circle is but a memory. We gave our best without regret, and there are homes in this country that will never again see the light that once shone around the fireside. But it will be a long and dark political night before the sun will rise upon the day that will see me again ally myself with that party which, when the fate of the nation was in the balance and the perils of war seemed about to overwhelm the Empire, refused to support the fullest measure of help that it lay within the power of the Dominion of Canada to give.
Mr. Speaker, I propose to vote against the amendment and with the Government.

Mr. Speaker, although the vitality of a nation must not be circumscribed in financial matters, yet these questions are daily taking a greater place in the life of humanity. Figures and numbers do not govern the world, but they are very useful to teach us how a nation is governed. The financial problems confronting our Dominion as a consequence of the war are of paramount importance, and during many years they will dominate our political life.
Canada's prosperity will mainly depend upon the solution given to those problems. It is then our duty to examine them in all their complexity, and to study very carefully the relations existing between the public finances, the private credit and the general economic organization of the country. When you consider, Sir, that our national net debt has increased fr6m $336,000,000 to $1,584,000,000 on March 31, 1919, and that it will amount to $1,950,000,000 in 1920, .which means an increase from $43,69 to

$220 per capita, and that the carrying charges on this debt have advanced from $1.96 per capita in 1913-14, to an estimated $15.33 per capita for the next fiscal year; when you find that every man, woman and child in the Dominion paid last year approximately $18.45 in customs taxes, the Government having collected $147,000,000 of customs duties and our population being approximately 8,000,000 people; when you ascertain that the cost of living has more than doubled, its increase being 115 per cent, and that the purchasing power of the dollar is gradually decreasing; when finally you have a deficit of $402,000,000 for the last fiscal year, and when you are told that for the next fiscal year there will be another enormous deficit; when you know that Canada will continue to live upon borrowings, you are amazed at the seriousness of our financial and economic situation, and as was said by a friend of the Government, you "cannot see where we are going to land unless it be in repudiation or bankruptcy," and if I rightly understood the hon. member (Mr. Stacey), I may add, in revolution.
What policy has the Government adopted to prevent such a calamity? Have the ministers been clearsighted? Have they spoken plainly, openly? Did they expedite matters with boldness and courage? No, Sir, on the contrary, they sheltered themselves and their responsibility behind commissions of which the weak point is to delay, more than is reasonable, useful solutions. We have the Commission on Labour and Industrial Unrest; and, Sir, the strikes are going on with all their troubles and disastrous consequences. We have the parliamentary Committee on the Cost of Living, appointed only at the end of this session. Finally, the Minister of Finance, in his Budget speech, tells us that we shall have a tariff inquiry, not now, but probably next fall. And yet all classes of society are anxious to have this question speedily settled.
It is time to clarify such a vitiated atmosphere, to reform these unfair practices if we wish to restore vitality and efficiency to our national organism. The people of ' Canada are sick and tired of commissions, inquries and reports, which, always ending only in speeches and gestures, indicate on the part of the Government their incapacity to conclude, move, and do something. The masses know that, in ordinary life, mediocre solutions coming in due time are preferable to perfect but tardy solutions. They feel that a firm and steady decision is more beneficial, chiefly in financial matters, than hesitation and contradiction. The Government should not forget that there is responsibility in inaction as well as in action. Moreover, responsibility in inaction is heavier, because inaction, under present circumstances, is synonymous with cowardice on the part of Government and engenders, in the masses discontent and Bolshevism.
The*most absorbing problem in our economic life is to determine how our Dominion will be able to create new capital and how we can extinguish first the currency inflation and then the fiscal inflation, so that we may come back as soon as possible to a lower cost of living. Reductions in the cost of living would involve a lowering of the cost of labour and of manufactured products, and then would favour an increase in internal consumption and the development of external trade. Speaking on the Budget, last year, I said:
The Government should cease to finance this country on paper. I warn them against the evils of such a policy. It will create further depreciation and economic tension. If they continue to increase this fiduciary circulation without adopting proper means to redeem it, they will make the trouble worse instead of better.
Unfortunately, the Government did not take these remarks into account, for our gold reserve, which was in August, 1914, 86 per cent of the total issue of $112,000,000, and 47 per cent in March, 1918, has been, according to the statements made by the Minister of Finance, reduced to 38.92 per cent in March, 1919, thus showing a decrease of 47.08 per cent since the outbreak of war. We are obliged to admit that our paper currency, particularly our Dominion currency, is in a state of inflation; that it is more and more watering, that our Dominion dollar is shrinking and that its purchasing power is lowering to a dangerous extent. The sole test of the dollar is what it will buy, and it rises and falls by that standard.
As stated by a correspondent of the Gazette, on March 10 last, "When- paper issues increase beyond the maximum requirements of circulation for domestic business purposes, prices of commodities increase in approximately the same degree; and the more irredeemable .paper issued, the greater the demand for currency to purchase commodities at the higher prices."
The same opinion was truly expressed by Mr. G. H. Cahan, in a letter published in the Financial Times on April 19 last. After having demonstrated that the basic circulating medium of the Government, which stood at $114,000,000 on June 30, 1914, has been diluted by the issue of an additional

issue of over $98,000,000 of irredeemable fiat currency, he adds:
It is a recognized economic law that such dilutions of the basic currency of a country inevitably decrease the purchasing power of money, or, in other words, increase the price of commodities; and this has undoubtedly occurred in Canada to some extent.
We think that a dollar is worth what it was when the war began in 1914. But it is not. The purchasing power of our dollar has decreased to 40 cents, as compared with pre-war prices, for the cost of living, according to statistics published by the Department of Labour, has increased by 115 per cent. The value of the purchasing power of our dollar, which is 40 cents, corresponds almost exactly with the amount of the gold guarantee that we have for each dollar and which is now 38.92 cents.
The Minister of Finance, who proudly says that the bank deposits in Canada almost doubled in the six years period from 1913 to 1919, should have added that this increase cannot be construed as evidence of an increase of wealth, and that it is more the result of currency inflation than of the people's savings. In reality, you have, it is true, $1,604,649,034 deposited in the hanks, but the purchasing power of this money being cut down to 40 per cent per dollar, as compared with pre-war prices, you can buy on that basis only $641,859,613 of goods, services or commodities; that is to say, $347,333,754 less than in 1913, since at that time we had bank deposits amounting to $988,191,367, and our dollar was not cut down to 40 cents hut had a full hundred cents purchasing power. Consequently -we can safely affirm that the national savings are more apparent than real; indeed, if you apply to them the test of purchasing power, they have fallen more than three hundred and forty millions of dollars since 1913. This is not to the credit of the 'Government, who, by their improvident policy of issuing irredeemable currency contrary to the law, have hypothecated the future of the country to an alarming extent, forgetting that monetary inflation, caused 'by the enormous development of governmental credit and emission of fiat currency, is not the proper means to obtain more goods and services, but constitutes, in reality, a deb t which must be liquidated sooner or later.
I entirely agiid! with the Minister of Finance when llm ! ays that " the policy will be to gradually instore our note issue to the statutory condition, which requires us to hold in gold tiyenty-five per cent up to [Mr. Trahan. 1
fifty million dollars of note issue, and dollar for dollar for any further issue." Further, I say that this should he done in the very near future. Great Britain has appointed a committee on currency and foreign exchanges after the war, to consider the various problems which will arise in connection with the currency and the foreign exchanges during the period of reconstruction, and report upon the steps required to bring about the restoration of normal conditions in due course. In Canada this work should he immediately done by the Treasury Board.
It is more than ever time for us to get back to sanity in matters of currency, because there is nothing more dangerous to the well-being of the people than inflation of money.
One of the most evident revolutionary ferments is the cost of living, the rise in price of all commodities necessary to life. It is also evident that the unlimited issue of currency notes has largely helped to modify the level of prices, and consequently, to aggravate the unrest.
According to a financier of world repute, Lord d'Abernon, " 80 per cent of the present industrial troubles and of Bolshevism " in England are due to the " enormous displacement in the value of the money;" he makes the further statement that " changes in the value of currency in which wages, salaries and other forms of remuneration are paid are the real cause of tl.e prevailing unrest."
We have the same conditions in our country; when the cost of living goes up more rapidly than salaries, we must not be surprised if the wage-earners are always asking for higher wages and go on strike in order to obtain a living wage.
We have two evils to combat: insufficiency of producers and the crowding of all kinds of middlemen beyond regular t;ade. The Government, instead of encouraging the former and of restraining the greed of the latter, has adopted as its panacea for solving all our war-problems the emiier course of manufacturing money; this policy was an inducement to profiteers to inciease their prices and has been the source of nearly all our labour unrest; and the Government must be held responsible for ihese monetary and fiscal inflations which have accentuated the hardships of th*i consumer by maintaining and keeping up the high cost of living. They deserve absolutely the criticism which the Economist of London applied to the British Government, on November 2 last, in the following terms:

" Thus the huge increase in paper money and bank credits, which has helped to push up prices, has swollen the cost of the war, and has caused an atmosphere of suspicion and unrest of which we may not yet have felt the full effects, is shown clearly to be due to the failure of our war Governments to get money in the right way, and their short-sighted abuses of their power of manufacturing money with the reluctant help of our bankers. If our Government had had the courage to take the money needed by taxation or forced loans instead of making new money and so depreciating the whole currency of the country, we should have been spared many an evil legacy which will complicate the after-war position."
I repeat, Sir, that we must come back to sanity in matters of currency if we sincerely desire to relieve the people by reducing the cost of living, and to prevent further labour unrest and troubles. It is our imperative duty, if we wish to attain these ends, to promote the deflation of our currency, even if such deflation were to be temporarily grievous, because it is better for our country to endure transitory difficulties than to enjoy a fictitious prosperity which will be the source of a permanent [DOT] crisis and may be the cause of repudiation, bankruptcy, or revolution.
What are the remedies for out present calamitous financial, economic and social situation. And does the Government intend to apply these remedies?
It is a recognized fact that the state expenditures are one of the main causes of inflation; hence, it is absolutely necessary that they should be minutely controlled in order to reduce them. The hon. member for Neepawa the other day recommended the establishment of a parliamentary national expenditure committee, such as there is in England, and I heartily approve of the suggestion. As stated by the London Economist, quoting the report of the British Committee on Currency: "Money needed for reconstruction purposes should not be provided by the creation of new credit, and, in so far as such expenditure is undertaken at all, it should be undertaken with great
caution	The shortage of real
capital must be made good by genuine savings. It cannot be met by the creation of fresh purchasing power in the form of bank advances to the Government, or to manufacturers under Government guarantee, or otherwise, and any resort to such expedients can only aggravate the evil and retard, possibly for generations, the recovery of the
country from the losses sustained during the war. A timely recognition of these homely truths would enable many wellmeaning gentlemen, who propose to cure all our post-war ills by multiplying money and credit instead of goods, to take a well-earned holiday, most beneficial to themselves and to the public."
Well, Sir, when you consider the enormous amount of expenditure for the present fiscal year you naturally try to find the reasons why these expenditures are progressively growing so rapidly and so unwisely. The answer is that the ministers have so great a love for big private interests that they lose sight of general and national interest. Instead of resolutely cutting down every expenditure which is not absolutely necessary, and of abandoning the policy followed in this country for many years, they adopt a policy of reckless extravagance, not in accordance with the financial and economic possibilities of Canada. Yet, the re-establishment of the equilibrium between revenue and expenditure with surpluses is necessary and more important than the execution of all philanthropic and financial schemes conceived by men saturated with the idea of governmental paternalism.
It is quite evident that the revenue necessary to meet the $438,000,000 required by the Government to provide for the expenditures mentioned in the Estimates, not including the amount required for demobilization, will not come from income or earnings, and that we will be obliged to cover the deficit by the creation of new credit, either by the issue of new currency, or by way of loans.
With the Weekly Sun, I am of the opinion that, under present circumstances, to borrow money to give employment at war wages upon unproductive public works such as highways, Welland canals, public buildings and railways, is not justifiable in the general interest. It merely defers for a short time an inevitable crisis in the relations between urban labour and capital, and tends to aggravate that crisis.
Nations are like individuals; when they have not sufficient financial resources to make improvements, they must delay them, especially if the country suffers from currency and fiscal inflation, which increase the cost of living and cause labour unrest.
If the Government was anxious to find a remedy for the abnormal situation actually confronting us, they should adopt a policy of curtailment of expenditures and set the example of economy. But, they prefer to

favour their good friends, the profiteers, to the detriment of the people, by accumulating deficits and increasing, for unproductive works, the national debt.
Government borrowings should 'cease at the earliest possible moment, if we wish to get rid of all these inflations, to reduce the cost of living, and to prevent more industrial unrest. The first way to realize these purposes is to proportion our expenditure to our revenue and to reduce the deficits. The Government has chosen another course, they are wasting money, they want to borrow again and again, and I charge them with being the direct cause of the unrest prevailing in the country, and which is largely due to the high cost of living resulting from currency, credit and fiscal inflations.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

When the
House rose at six o'clock I was saying that if the Government was anxious to remedy the grave evils confronting our Dominion, and consisting in the high cost of living and labour unrest, its duty was to stop borrowing, make the expenditure correspond to the revenue, permit the deflation of currency, and take all proper measures to lessen the'fiscal inflation.
Another remedy to cure the existing evils would be to increase our production and our export trade,

which brings me to the tariff question.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey) stated this afternoon that in view of the fact that there existed in Canada the menace of revolution and general unrest all over the Dominion, it was no time to discuss the tariff question, and for that reason he would vote against the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brome and in support of the Government. May I be permitted to tell the hon. gentleman that as the Government, by its policy of inaction, is directly responsible for the existing general labour unrest, he would have good ground for voting against it, because he himself says that that unrest is a bad thing for Canada.
As a Liberal I am theoretically a free trader because, as Cobden said, "Free trade is the best factor for peace." Sir, respect for liberty, property, peace and harmony will only exist when men rise to that level of international morality evidenced by eco-

nomic co-operation, and which consists in the free exchange of the commodities necessary to life. Otherwise, humanity is greatly exposed to fiscal tyranny and to the injustice which characterizes its operation. I may add with Mr. George Evan Putman, president of the American Free Trade League, that "if we repudiate Prussianism we must also repudiate its brother, Protectionism:" But, Sir, taking into consideration the new conditions created by the war, the enormous debt and the annual charges which confront us, we must all admit that it is altogether impossible to have, for the present, absolute free trade in Canada. It would be also more dangerous to continue the practice of adequate protection in our commercial relations with other countries. It is sufficient to quote the maxim of free trade:	Laissez faire,
laissez passer,"-"Let do, let pass," and to bear in mind the imperative "Produce and export," which must be the programme of this Dominion, to understand that in the future the mere application of either protection or free trade in its entirety would become more and more difficult. A judicious, practical, and patriotic opportunism must, above all during the new era of reconstruction, actuate and direct every true Canadian in the most noble enterprises for the economic renovation of this Dominion. We must of necessity have sufficient revenue to pay the interest on our war loans, the pensions to our soldiers, and the ordinary expenditure, without being obliged to resort to new borrowings.
Consequently we may without any protectionist views, but only for fiscal purposes, provide a part of the necessary revenue by way of fiscal duties, but it cannot be a question of protective or prohibitive duties. There is antagonism between fiscal and protective duties. The former, which exist in 'England, the classical land of commercial freedom, have for their sole object the providing of revenue for the treasury; they are not intended to prohibit the entrance of certain products, or to raise the prices of certain national products. On the contrary, the protective duties are naturally prohibitive. President McKinley said that they are not designed to increase the national revenue, but by prohibiting the importation of the protected products to reduce, or to even suppress revenue.
We have now adequate protection, and the Budget proposals do not alter our protective duties. Bearing in mind that after having first of all provided generously for the home consumption of natural products,

we are bound to increase our own export trade if we want to accumulate national wealth and to have a better rate of exchange-as is well known, the present rate of exchange against Canada is 3 per centr- considering that the development of our export trade is in direct proportion to the Liberalism of our tariff, and that in matters of external trade the rule "Do ut des"- "give in order to receive"-is rigorous and strict, that industrial progress to be satisfactory should not strangle agriculture- which is intrinsically essential to this country and must be developed to the utmost in order to have a prosperous Canada-I enthusiastically support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brome, which embodies the policy of the Liberal party and the claims of the farmers of this country, as regards reduction of the customs tariff, free food, free agricultural implements, and the revival of the reciprocity agreement. This amendment constitutes a step forward in the right direction, and every one admits that in this matter we must proceed gradually but surely.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Car-vell) and many other members have asked this House, where we are going to get the extra revenue which we shall require to meet the state expenditure. They speak of an estimated annual deficit of $100,000, 000. Would it not be more proper, Sir, to look carefully into the Estimates, to examine seriously the various proposals made by the Government, in order to ascertain if it is not possible to economize and practice the thrift so eloquently preached by the ministers on the treasury benches? What we should do in the future is to refrain from extravagant and wasteful expenditure. I venture to say, Sir, that the Government could have saved this year the estimated deficit of $100,000,000 by putting off the shipbuilding programme, $30,000,000; the housing scheme, $25,000,000; the highways vote, $25,000,000; by not granting to the soldiers so generous a bonus, which, according to one of their best friends is " absolutely absurd and ill-considered," and will cost millions and millions of dollars; by not assuming the deficits of the Canadian Northern railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway; by making reductions in the number of civil servants; by abolishing the information bureau and the Canadian Official Record. If the Government followed this policy of retrenchment we would not have to face deficits and we would not be obliged to borrow to the detriment of this country.
As to the income tax, Sir, I may say that it should be the incumbent and necessary correction of the fiscal duties. But I regret that it is much lessened by the fact that the Victory bonds are exempt from taxation, and I may ask, with the Financial Times, " What is the good of an income tax if the incomes on $1,250,000,000 to $1,500,000,000 is not to be taxed?" For my part I say: Away with tax exemption. And I sternly blame the Government, as I did last year, for .having exempted such bonds from taxation. This is an unjust policy, and to illustrate that I wish to put in Hansard two extracts which, to my mind, prove conclusively how great has been the mistake of the Government in adopting such a course. The first extract is taken from the Labour World of August last year.
This paper is the organ of labour in the city of Montreal, and the article that I quote is entitled:
The Income Tax, a toon for the rich. A legislation which enables profiteers to accumulate therir gains instead of forcing them to bear their share of the burden imposed by the war.
The article reads:
The law, as it stands now, provides for the taxation of excess profits and surplus of revenue over a certain definite amount, but provides also for the exemption of all money invested in war bonds or war charities. And of course, every practical financier will invest in war bonds bearing a fair rate pf interest all the money that otherwise the government would seize for war purposes. The excess profits, instead of being confiscated, as it was intended by the Income Tax Act, is being borrowed by the Government, and the mass of the people will have to pay the interest on same later. Thus instead of relieving the poor it adds to their burden.
By the tax exemption on investment in war issues, these bonds are as good to a man with a $6,000 yearly income as would any other investment at 5.7S per cent. To a man having an income of $12,000 per year these bonds are as good as another investment yielding 6.10 per cent. To a $80,000' a year income, they are worth 7.47 per cent. To a $500;000 income, they are worth 11.61 per cent and to a $1,000,000 income these bonds are worth 20.2>9 per cent.
I may say that these calculations were made under the old law. If they were made) on the new rates proposed in the Budget, the rates of interest on these bonds would be higher:
Moreover every one agrees that our income taxes are most likely to increase in which case the above figures will be more discriminating.
As these bonds are only worth 55 per cent to the man whose income is less than $2,000' a year, it is obvious that tax exemption in that case as in any other case, becomes class favouritism. Well, class favouritism is the very thing that this war is intended to abolish and which we all strive to strike out. Class favouritism does not exist at the front, why should it be main-

tain&d at the rear? The poor' have readily given their lives for the defence of the country and civilization; they have contributed to a large extent to the various patriotic enterprises and war relief funds. The rich are still evading their duty, though they appear to be very generous. They want compulsion for all except for themselves, and when investing their profits in war bonds they are being credited with patriotic instincts, although it is a means of escaping taxation.
It may be said that this extract comes from a radical source. I have thought proper to quote another extract coming from another source, from a financial paper, the Financial Times, of Montreal, the organ of many financiers in that city, in an article published on August 3, last, said:
Great Britain and' the United States tried the tax-exempt bonds, but found that the exemption was not necessary. Patriotism in those countries apparently was not to be measured by interest bonus or tax exemption. Those countries did not underestimate the spirit of their people.
As the present Government has done by adopting the policy it has adopted regarding these bonds.
The future danger of present tax-exempt bonds is the danger of permanently high rates of interest. General interest rates always pivot around the prevailing rate of Government bonds. Government bonds provide the yield basis upon which all moneys for social (municipal service and Industrial development are borrowed. Whatever a government bond yields, the graded securities must regulate their interest yield accordingly. Money borrowed for purposes of the pulp mill, the steel works, the street railway or the school hoard, must be borrowed' at a rate which will appear attractive in comparison with government bonds.
Therefore, a load' of tax-exempted bonds will have some very serious possibilities: it relieves the rich man of a definite duty towards the State; it places the onus of taxation upon the poor man (by indirect taxation on necessities) ; it raises the rates on money for industrial enteiprise, the effect of which would be to make money so expensive that further development would he checked; and it puts a price and a prize on patriotism when no price or prize is asked.
If we all are equally to share the burden of the cost of freeing the world from the Prussian influence, we cannot do it by exempting from taxation a billion dollars or more of the money spent in the fulfilment of that purpose. The word exemption should be taboo. It does not fit this democracy.
I hope the bearers of these bonds will follow the advice given to them by the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), when addressing the West-mount Canadian Club, he said:
Many people made money during the war and tucked it away in Viotory Bonds. Unless some one is ready to loosen a little of that money in order to tide over the situation, that

is to say, to provide employment-well, just think about it.
I hope also that the Government will adopt a better method in negotiating our next domestic loan.
There seems to be a consensus of opinion that the income tax must be collected on a graduated scale. It is necessary to guard strictly against false declarations by the taxpayers, otherwise the income tax may be a tax on honesty, the honest taxpayer paying while the clever hypocrite evades the tax, and owing to an important political situation the latter is assured the benevolence of the Administration. The income tax must more and more admit of a system of wide publicity. Public opinion has the right to exercise an efficient control over the participation of every citizen in the national taxation. I therefore respectfully suggest that an annual report should be made to Parliament in the first ten days of the session, giving the name and residence of the taxpayer, the class in which his income falls, the amount of income tax paid, and the amount exempted. Some may object that secrecy or privacy is necessary in business. But these objectors are the first to go to mercantile or information agencies and make inquiries on the financial standing of the industries, contemplate dealing. After all, we must recognize that the actual situation of everyone in his relation to the public treasury should be known by the public; not in full detail, but that we may know the class in which he should be placed according to his own declaration. In my humble opinion this would be an excellent method of preventing false and fraudulent declarations.
Another class of people who often try to evade the income tax are the holders of shares, bonds, debentures, and other personal or moveable property. To prevent these evasions I would urge the Government to establish a system of registration so that each owner of bonds, shares or other personal property would be obliged to register against his name the amount of his personal property, and in case of sale the transfer would be noted under the name of the new owner. A penalty should be imposed for non-compliance with the law, and in case of recidivism, such moveable property, that is to say, shares, bonds, debentures, etc., should be confiscated. I believe this method would to a certain degree settle the action of moveable capital, limit its power, prevent evasions of the Income Tax Act, and facilitate the work of the tax collector. Moreover, every person should be compelled to make a return show-

ing whether or not he is liable under the Income Tax Act, and the names of those making fraudulent declarations should be published. We should also adopt the distinction made in England between earned and unearned income.
I sincerely believe that if these suggestions were adopted and put into practice the income tax, which yielded only ten million dollars last year, would produce a much greater revenue. One word more on this question. The Minister of Finance was right when he said that " carried beyond a reasonable point," the income tax " can only defeat its purpose, with consequences detrimental to capital, labour, and the community as a whole." Why? Because it would then become a cause of rack for the ratepayer, a device to an arbitrary distribution of wealth, and at length a great factor of impoverishment. I notice that the tax on the smaller incomes has been increased by one hundred per cent, and I would ask the Government to reduce the tax for this class.
In conclusion, let me say that the Budget proposals are not satisfactory. They do not attempt in the slightest degree to solve for the benefit of the masses the problems of the cost of living and industrial unrest. On the contrary, by the inflation of national expenditures, by adding further to our currency inflation, by increasing the cost of living, they will aggravate existing evils and cause greater labour unrest. The Government, instead of practising financial wisdom, that is to say, moderation in expenditure, prudence in taxation, and a stubborn struggle against the increasing of the national debt, lavishly spends public money, accumulates deficits and borrowings, manufactures new money and credits to encourage profiteers, and dislocates our national finances. In matters of fiscal policy they always " wait and see," forgetting that if they desire to avoid new and greater catas-trophies and disasters their duty now is first to be clear-sighted, then to speak plainly and openly, if they have ideas, and finally to be courageous enough to act quickly. But they prefer to postpone solutions and to continue, on this tariff question, to bilk ideas and facts with words.
Well Sir, we on this side of the House strongly condemn this sluggish and suspicious attitude of the Government. We emphatically declare that at the present juncture there is not a more imperative and solemn duty than the accumulation of national wealth in 'Canada. It is a sacred duty in the interests of the families who have contributed their best manhood to the

cause of the Allies and have shed bloody tears during the past years of trial. There is no more sacred duty than the careful preparation for the future of our country and the ensuring of its permanent prosperity. There is no more sacred duty before us than to provide employment for the returned soldiers as soon as they are reestablished in civil life. There is no more sacred duty to our beloved Canada than to enable her at the earliest possible moment to pay the heavy debts that she has incurred in order to assure the triumph of liberty and right. It is a sacred duty, if moral and social order will prevail in our country, to make an earnest appeal to every true and faithful Canadian to join in a patriotic movement to the end that we may promote the welfare of Canada and realize in the result national strength and national unity.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELiL (President of the Privy Council): Mr. Speaker, I shall not attempt to refer at any length to the remarks of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Trahan). He has criticised the financial administration of this country during the war, and as I followed his observations, two of the main points of his criticism appeared to be, first, the inflation of the country's currency, and secondly, the extent and character of our borrowings. Just a word in reference to this in passing. My hon. friend, who appears to have made some study of this question, must recognize the fact that inflation of currency is, to some extent at least, inseparably associated with a war such as that we have just passed through. But I believe that the records will show that Canada has less inflation of her currency than any other country that entered the war at the time we did. I desire to pay my tribute to the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) for the splendid manner in whibh the finances of Canada have been managed during this war. I think that when you compare 'Canada's financial record in the war with the record of any other country, it will be conceded that no Government can show a better record of judicious handling of the country's finances, and that in no other country have the people responded more readily to the appeals of the Government for financial support in carrying on the war.
Just one word with reference to the borrowings of the country. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) touched on this point, and he suggested that the Victory bonds had got into the hands of a few

capitalists and were exempt from taxation. That was the substance of a portion at least of the complaint he had to make. I think my hon. friend, in speaking as he did, could not have had in mind the actual facts of the situation. In the Victory Loan of 1917 there were no fewer than 820,035 subscribers, and in the loan of 1918 no feweT than 1,067,879 subscribers. Now, Mr. Speaker, when we recognize the fact that many of these subscribers were heads of families, it is apparent that the number of subscribers represents a very much larger percentage of the population of Canada than the actual number of names, and I venture to think that if we could trace out the number of families represented, we would find somewhere from a quarter to a half of the entire population of Canada directly interested in the Victory bonds subscribed for in the last loan. I am not going to enter into a discussion to-night of the question as to whether or not bonds should be exempt from taxation, but I wish to point . out that these bonds are in possession not of the rich alone. The rich have some, but these bonds are owned by all classes of people throughout the entire country.
Is it not a fact that a large number of these bonds have since changed hands and gone into possession of large investors?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My information is that
comparatively few have changed hands. The people do not wish to sell them. The credit of the country is so good that the people are glad to have the bonds. But whether they have changed hands or not, the fact is: The terms upon which a loan is put on the market govern the price at which it will be taken and the extent of the subscription which will be made to it. And in putting this loan upon the market, the Finance Minister, having regard to the condition of the market and the demands which had been made upon the Canadian people, considered that the terms were fair to the subscribers, fair to the people as a whole and were such as would ensure that the Government would get the money necessary to carry on the war, and maintain our forces at the front. So far as the work of the Minister of Finance is concerned, I have had an intimate knowledge of it only during the' past eighteen months, but I have generally observed it during the three and a half years preceding, and I want to say that I do not know of any finance minister of any country at war who has handled the finances of the

country better and has achieved finer results than has the present Minister of Finance. These are the only observations I intend to make with reference to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Trahan).
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) I would like to make two or three observations which I am sure the hon. gentleman will not take amiss. I have always listened to him with the greatest interest and have always been able to gather valuable information from his addresses. But I must confess that to-day I did not think that either in the substance or in the manner of his deliverance he was equal to his best efforts in this House and elsewhere, and I felt it was due to the fact that he was not on wholly sound ground in a portion of his address.
He was trying to say a good word for you.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member always has a good word to say for the Union Government because he recognizes its merits. My hon. friend's criticisms of the Government's fiscal policy as I recall them, laid special emphasis on two points, apart from the general discussion of protection and free trade, into which I do not intend to enter. First, he criticised the duties on food, and discussed at considerable length and with great force the importance of food supply and also the high cost of living. In connection with that argument he made two points. First, his argument was that the duty should have been wholly removed from foodstuffs; and second that the high prices of food in Canada were not due to any shortage of food in this country. He held that we had an abundance of food in Canada, and attributed the high prices to the hoarding of food and excessive profits made by the profiteers. Let me say in passing, that if the food is in the country and if the scarcity of it and the high prices are due to the two causes mentioned, 1 confess that personally I cannot see how the removal of the duty would have stopped hoarding or affected prices. I deeply regret for many reasons, but to-night particularly for the reason I am about to mention, that my hon. friend the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has retired from the Government. It is a matter of deep regret to all his colleagues, and especially to me, because our relations have been the most cordial and sympathetic from the day we entered the Government together. But 1 wish my hon. friend had been in my place here to-night to defend his adminis-

tration in relation to the prices o! food and the work of the Canada Food Board. I am sure the hon. member for Red Deer did not realize that this afternoon he was delivering a strong criticism of the administration of my hon. friend the former Minister of Agriculture.
He was in charge of the food board and of all -these regulations during the past fifteen months. The food board under the administration of my hon. friend the exMinister of Agriculture, did take steps to. deal with hoarding; they did take steps to cut down excessive profits; they did take steps to protect the public. I believe that my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture took such steps as he believed to be effective and as he believed to be in the public interest. My hon. friend the exMinister of Agriculture will agree that he never submitted any proposals to the Government, he never made any proposition to his colleagues, to regulate the price of food and to prevent hoarding or to limit profits, that his colleagues did no1! most cordially support. He had the backing of his colleagues in connection with every effort he put forth in this direction.
If there was any friend of the food profiteers in the Government, i't must necessarily have been my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture and I think it is only necessary to state the proposition to convince the House and the country of the absurdity of the suggestion no matter from what quarter it may emanate.
I do not want to pry into Cabinet secrets, but I would like to know if my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) ever suggested taking the tariff off foodstuffs?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know that my hon.
friend (Mr. Michael Clark) is very able and very clever but I was dealing with the proposition which my hon. friend put forth when he said that the high cost of food in this country was due to hoarding and excessive profits.
Answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let us keep to the
point under discussion and I will deal with the other question when the time comes. Confining ourselves to this question, what I am saying to the House, to the . country and to my hon. friend is: My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture had charge of that branch of the public service. He administered it
with great efficiency. If there was any failure it was failure on his part to recommend to his colleagues what further steps . should be taken, but.I do not believe that there was any failure on his part. He did his duty as he saw it with the results that we see in the country to-day.
You are not very complimentary to your former colleague.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
desires to address the House he should do the House the courtesy of rising and addressing the Chair.

Mr. Speaker, we were asked a question from the other side of the House.
I said it would be more complimentary to the former colleague of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rowell) not to discuss Cabinet secrets before the hon. ex-Minister of Agriculture resigned.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not discussing secrets;
I am stating facts. Then, let me refer to' some of the measures taken to deal with this matter. I only touch upon them because I know that my hon. friend from Red Deer wishes to be fair and does not wish to misrepresent the position of the Government one iota. Take the question of the profits of the big packers and cold storage men which has been so much discussed in this House. What was done under the administration of by hon. friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture? Regulations were imposed which, in the first place, limited the profits on the turnover of the leading cold storage men and packers. They were required under regulations, which were administered by the Government, and under license issued by the Department of Agriculture, or the Food Board-I forget which-to so carry on their business that their profits should not exceed two per cent on their turnover. Notwithstanding that, if they earned a profit on the capital invested in the business of over 7 per cent, and up to 15 per cent, one-half over 7 per cent went to the Gov-9 p.in. eminent as revenue, and the other half went to the packer. [DOT] All over 15 per cent went to the Government. The result was that no packer could earn more than 11 per cent on his total actual capital invested in the business, and he was subject to the business war profits tax as well. The packers very strongly resisted these regulations and protested against them. We are sometimes asked the question:	"Why
has not the Government done as the American Government has done in regulating the packers and controlling food prices?" The

Government under the administration of the ex-Minister of Agriculture has gone farther than the American Government in regulating and controlling profits and prices. Our regulations have been far more drastic and far-reaching than those of the American Government. What has been the position of the American Government in dealing with this same matter? They allowed packers whose turnover was less than $100,000,000, which would include all our packers, a profit of 2i per cent on their turnover, with no limitation whatever upon the profit on actual capital invested in the business. Those whose turnover exceeded $100,000,000 were allowed a certain percentage on the capital invested in the business. The limitation varied according to the character of the particular branch of the business carried on but by a coincidence it figured out that the profits of the four big packing houses of the United States were limited to 11 per cent on the capital. Under the American regulations capital included borrowed money, so that the American packers were able to earn eleven per cent not only on the capital invested in the business but on money borrowed, as well. The Canadian packers protested against our regulations. They said, in the first place, you are imposing a greater limitation on the annual turnover than is imposed upon the packers in a similar position in the United States, and then you are adding to that limitation a further serious restriction upon the actual earnings of the packers, a restriction even stricter than that imposed in the United States upon the four big packers. In other words, this Government combined the limitations and regulations which the American Government imposed on both classes of packers upon our packers, and made them far more stringent. It is under this system that the packers of this country have carried on their business since January, 1918. In no country at war have such stringent regulations been imposed upon the packers and cold storage people as have been imposed by the Government on the packers of this country.
When my hon. friends talk of this Government being the friend of food profiteers-I am not speaking of my hon. friend from Red Deer, but of some hon. gentlemen opposite-they are speaking either without a knowledge of the facts or for political effect; they are misrepresenting the situation, and I say that at this time any hon. member who falsely charges the Government with standing in with the food profiteers, when there is such

a feeling of unrest throughout the country, is only contributing and adding to that unrest which may shake the foundations of government in Canada.

Did this Government take any means, either on their own behalf, or on behalf of the British Government, to recover from certain packing houses in this country the value of the post-cured bacon-salt water pumped into the bacon uselessly and for which the British taxpayer had to pay?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend's remark is about as relevant as his remarks usually are to the subject under discussion. The Government took whatever action the British Government required in all matters that related to the administration of British affairs in this country.
Coming to the situation in Great Britain, my hon. friend mentioned that the price of bacon was lower in Great Britain than it was here. I do not know, that may be the case; but there is this fact which the House and the country should keep in view. The British Government adopted a policy, which this Government has not adopted. Men may differ on it, some may think that this Government should have adopted it, but personally I do not think that the situation in this country called for its [DOT] adoption. The British Government undertook to look after the feeding of the British people, and the British Government purchased the food. All purchases were made on behalf of the British Government. It all came in through the Government, the Government distributed it throughout the country, sold much of it to the people of Britain at less than cost and charged up the difference as part of the war expenditure.
That is one reason why certain classes of food can be sold cheaper in Great Britain than they can in Canada-the British people are paying for it as part of war expenditure, I doubt very much if the people of Canada would sustain the Government in paying to the farmers and producers of the Dominion a price in excess of the regular price, and selling it at a substantially lower figure. But what I say is this: If that is a wise policy it was not recommended by my hon. friend. He is a pretty good judge on these mattters, and I would depend on his judgment. Notwithstanding the fact that the British Government is to-day buying this food, and has been for the past two years; notwithstanding that the British Government is selling it to the people of Britain at less than cost, paying the difference out of the exchequer; notwithstanding

that Great Britain is a free trade country, and has been during all the period my hon. friend has mentioned, the cost of living in free trade Great Britain, with food partially paid for by the Government, is higher today to the average man than it is in the Dominion of Canada. Now that is no argument against free trade.
It is a perfectly general statement as to which my friend has no proof.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All I can say In proof of the statement is this: I have discussed the matter with those who have been over in Great Britain looking after our trade interests, as well as with the Prime Minister of Canada (Sir Robert Borden). They have had special occasion to look into the question with a view of developing Canadian trade; they had to consider the price at which goods were being sold in Great Britain-foodstuffs of all kinds and manufactured articles-with a view of seeing how far Canada could compete in the British markets; and the one testimony they have all brought back -is that at the present time the cost of living is higher in Great Britain than in Canada and that we can sell our goods in the British market at a profit. That is the basis for my observation. -
Now, let me turn to another matter which my hon. friend mentioned. One of the important points discussed in his address, was the question of what should be the policy of the Government with reference to the iron and steel and the coal industries. If I rightly understood my hon. friend he took the logical and consistent position, from his standpoint, that all duties, all protection, should be removed from these industries, and that if -they could not live under those conditions they did not deserve to exist. If I have in any way misapprehended my hon. friend in that respect I would be very glad if he would correct me. I understand him to admit that I have correctly stated his position, and such being the case, there are two or three facts I should like to bring to his attention which appear to me to have a very important bearing on this matter. My hon. friend will recollect that one of the most important and most valuable industries in Canada during the war was that of the manufacture of munitions. The British Government expended in Canada something like $1,000,000,000 first through the Shell Committee, and then through the Imperial Munitions Board, for the purchase of shells and other munitions. Mr. Speaker, the people of
this country do not realize how large a factor the pouring of those millions into all channels of trade in Canada was in our industrial operations, and how it has contributed to Canada's ability to bear the burden of this war. If we had not had that immense expenditure of public money, Canada at this time would have been in a very serious position financially. I am not going to argue on the merits or demerits of protection and free trade; I am simply dealing with the facts. That munitions industry could not have been carried on in this country if we had not had iron and steel and coal industries here. This is not a theory we are dealing with, it is an actual condition. You may agree, or disagree, with the theory of protection and free trade, but I repeat that we could not have carried on the munitions industry without our iron and steel and coal industries in Canada.
Then I want to go a step further. When the United States entered the war we found it practically impossible to get the necessary steel, the necessary raw materials in certain lines, to provide the amount required for our domestic uses. We faced this situation at one time during the war-the public did not know it, because it could not be disclosed to them-the railway companies of Canada claimed that their tracks were in such a condition that they were a menace to the travelling public, and yet they could not better their position for the reason that they could not get the rails necessary to relay the tracks. Why could they not get rails? Because to get them we would have had to stop the manufacture of steel for munitions, and it was a choice between continuing the supply of shells for overseas or making the rails to renew railroad tracks in [DOT] this country. Every pressure was used to increase the output of steel. As a matter of fact, under the pressure of necessity, the output of steel in Canada was doubled during the war. A colleague sitting beside me states that it was more than doubled and I will accept his statement. Notwithstanding that there was this pressure I have mentioned, it was only after the utmost efforts that some relief was secured, by buying rails which had been sold to Russia, but which she had failed to take. We also, after great effort, secured certain rails in the Unitea States. Then, by the most persistent pressure through the War Trade Board here, and through the War Trade Mission in Washington, headed by Mr. Lloyd Harris, we got some further relief to supplement the steel required to carry on our industrial

operations. Every iron and steel plant, every plant depending on iron and steel in Canada, was living from hand to mouth for weeks at a time, and I wish to say now that, so far as I am concerned, it is not a question of protection and free trade, it is a question of national safety and national defence. I am going to stand for a policy that will make Canada self-contained, so far as possible, in connection with the iron and steel industry. So long as I am a member of this House I am not prepared * to see Canada again in the position she was during the war because we did not have this basic industry adequately developed. I believe that what is true of iron and steel is equally true of coal. We know about the coal shortage, and we know all that it involved. In respect of iron and steel and coal, so far as is practicable, Canada should ibe self-contained. But I add to that declaration, Mr. Speaker, that if the iron and steel industry needs to be further developed in order that we may be self-contained, it should be accompanied by such regulations as would prevent men making an excessive profit out of it. 60 far as I am concerned that is the policy I intend to stand for. I believe we require it in the interests of the nation for the protection of our national life. But we will see to it that the industry shall be carried on under such conditions that excessive profits will not be made by those engaged in it.
Now, if my hon. friend will permit me, I will turn from his address and touch on some other matters which have been discussed in this debate. From the very nature of the issues in this war, from the forces engaged on either side, from the weapons of destruction used, and having regard to the period over which the war extended, certain results have inevitably followed. But the same results have inevitably followed in every other country that was at war; they are not peculiar to Canada, they are worldwide. Let me mention three or four. First, a heavy public debt, an inevitable result of the war; second, high cost of living, an inevitable result of the war; third, industrial unrest, an inevitable result of the war. Fourth, as a result of the strain and stress of the war almost the whole nation is suffering from neurasthenia.
Let us look at these inevitable results of the war for a few minutes. First, the national debt; what is it? The Finance Minister has pointed out that by the end of next year Canada will have a national debt of not

less than $1,950,000,000. An enormous debt for a country like Canada, and yet less, having regard to our ability to pay, than that of any country at war except the United States. And having regard to the character and ability of our people and of our great national resources, I am sure that with unity and courage we can face that task and accomplish it without serious difficulty.
But what is entailed by that public debt? This year it is estimated that the interest on it will be $102,000,000. The cost of pensions1 will be $30,000,000. We have already voted for soldiers' re-establishment, to assist in the retraining of our soldiers and the care of those disabled, $22,763,000. Those three sums represent a total this year on current account of $154,000,000, and there may have to be something added in the Supplementary Estimates. Now, I ask the House-and this must be viewed in the light of actual conditions-to compare that with the ordinary expenditure of Canada before the war. Our highest expenditure for the year 1913-14 was $127,384,000. We face this year on current account an actual expenditure for those three items of $25,000,000 more than the total expenditure on current account in the year preceding the war.
Then take not only the current expenditure this year, but the expenditure on war account. The estimated expenditure on war account this year is $300,000,000. Our total expenditure on war account for the year 1915-16 was $166,197,755; for 1914-15 it was only $60,000,000. But suppose I take 1915-16, because that has been referred to as the year this war tariff was put on. Our expenditure on war account this year is practically double our expenditure on war account in the year when this additional tariff was put on for war purposes.
Now, why have I referred to these items? For the reason that the Finance Ministei was within the judgment of this House and of the country when he said that so far as finance is concerned this is a war year. This is vastly more a war year than the year when the duty was put on. Both our capital and our current expenditure on account of the war are vastly greater than they weTe during the year that duty was put on. Therefore, if it ever could be justified-I am not now saying it can; I am not now discussing it-as a measure to raise revenue in aid of the war, it could be absolutely justified during the present year.
I want to say to the House that I entirely share the view of the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization, that

when this House met, the Finance Minister might have said: This is a war year, and the finance this year must be war finance. The question of a revision, of the tariff must stand over until this war year is over. The Union Government was not formed for the purpose of dealing with that issue. He might have stated that to the House and the country, and I would have stood side by side with my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization in support of that position. And I am dealing perfectly fairly with all my friends and colleagues when I say that there would have been no dissent from that proposition by any member of the Government. The Finance Minister could have come down to this House with that policy and a united Government would have faced the House and the country in support of it.
When the House met, our friends from Western Canada, including my hon. friend from Red Deer, pressed most strongly that the Government should not pursue that course, and they urged that there should be at least some reductions in the tariff.
I am sure that every member of the House recognized that it was not possible to have a thorough revision this year, no matter how anxious the Government might have been to undertake it. If any hon. member questions that statement let me call to the attention of the House one or two facts in the situation. What was the position when it was known publicly that the armistice was likely to be signed? The Prime Minister was called overseas to attend the Peace Conference. He went, because all his colleagues thought that that was where he should be. I was glad that my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) last night frankly stated that that is where the Prime Minister should have been, and that if he had not been there my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) would have demanded that he should have been there to represent Canada. But I say to the IHlouse and to the country, if the Prime Minister had not gone overseas to represent Canada at the Peace Conference, how this Government would have been denounced for neglecting Canada's interests in the greatest conference ever held among the nations. And the House will learn, when the time comes for the Prime Minister to make his statement, how greatly Canada has benefited by his presence at the Conference, and how seriously Canada might have suffered in many proposals that came before the Conference if she had not been represented by
her Prime Minister, with authority to speak for the whole [DOT] nation and to insist that Canada's rights and interests should be protected.
The Prime Minister was overseas necessarily attending the Peace Conference, he was where duty called him and the country demanded he should be, and the ministers at home were as busily engaged as they could possibly be in dealing with problems here at home-I ask how was it possible for any Government in the absence of the Prime Minister, with the conditions under which we were working, to make such an investigation of the tariff as would make possible a thorough revision this year? There is not a thoughtful member of this House-and 1 put it up to the conscience of the members, and particularly of those on this side of the House-who would say that it is humanly possible for the Government, since the armistice was signed and with the Prime Minister overseas, to radically change the fiscal policy of the country and thoroughly revise the tariff, and at the same time bring down new and radical taxation proposals to make up the revenue. It could not be done. If, therefore, it was not possible for the Government to make a thorough revision of the tariff this session-and hon. members will concede that it was not-how can hon. members who are supporters of the Government vote against it because it has not achieved the impossible. When our hon. friends came down from the West-and some from the East, too-they urged that something should be done this session-that, at least, the tariff war tax of 7i per cent and 5 per cent should be taken off. I do not hesitate to say that I urged my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to endeavour to meet this view. Every man must exercise his own judgment on an important issue like this, and I have the greatest respect for the judgment and sincerity of my hon. friend the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar; but I say to the House and to the country that if I was prepared, as all my colleagues were, to support the Finance Minister in coming down to this 'House during this war year without any revision of the tariff, I do not believe that I am absolved from supporting him when he has revised the tariff in a measure according to the lines that I desire. I feel there is a double obligation upon myself to stand by the Minister of Finance and my other colleagues who have made a partial revision in the tariff along lines which I believe to be just and right in the .public interest.

I am particularly pleased with certain aspects of the Government's tariff proposals. I want to join with the hon. member for Red Deer (iMr. M. Clark) in expressing appreciation of the Government's tariff proposal to the extent to which it increases the British preference. From the standpoint, not only of our national position, but of the economic position of Canada, one of the wisest features of the Budget of 1897, the Fielding tariff of 1897, was the provision for the British preference. I thought so then; I have always thought so since, and I am glad that this Budget carries us a little further along the line of British preference. I do not know what the investigation next autumn will show when it is undertaken, but I earnesly hope it will show that it may be possible to increase that preference without seriously interfering with established industries in Canada.
I am glad of the provision that does go a certain distance towards removing the duty on foodstuffs. When the revision takes place, I hope it may be possible to go further, I am sure the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the hon. member for Red Deer will both agree that it is difficult to draw conclusions from general statements unless one knows all the facts. Let me mention the case which the hon. member for Marquette mentioned yesterday about the Dominion Textile Company and the large profits they had earned. Yesterday, by a strange coincidence, Sir Charles Gordon, president of that company, happened to be in my office, before my hon. friend had spoken. Some question came up about this announcement in the paper showing their large profits, and Sir Charles told me that more than 50 per cent of the profit was made owing to the increase in value of raw cotton and other raw material they had on hand during the year. In other words, they had bought at a fortunate time; they had exercised good judgment in buying; the price of raw materials had gone up, and that resulted in more than one-half of the total profits they made. I am not mentioning that except for this point, namely, that if we are to adjust the tariff, having regard to preserving so far as is feasible, consistently with the public interest, existing manufacturing institutions, we must carefully look into the facts before we reach conclusions. That is my sole reason for mentioning this matter. If it is suggested that they earned these large profits because there was a tariff on those goods, I point out to my hon. friends that in to-day's Montreal Gazette, by another coincidence, is a list

of the dividends paid by the British cotton companies during this past year, and it shows that the majority of the cotton companies in Free Trade England made on their capital stock a much larger profit than did the Dominion Textile Company in Canada. It is not necessary for me to trouble the House with the details which I have here, but the profits made on the capital stock run up to 90 per cent. That is no argument against free trade. It only shows that owing to war conditions
Did the gentleman connected with the Dominion Textile Company inform the President of the Council how much watered stock was provided for in declaring the dividend of 31 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I did not discuss that with him; I was discussing only this point. But even that again would show the importance of investigation in order to find out the facts.
In the third place, I am glad to support this Budget because, as the hon. member for Red Deer has so well pointed out-probably some of my colleagues on this side of the House may not agree with me-it embodies and puts in permanent form those items in the reciprocity agreement of 1911 which I deemed of most importance and in respect of which I most strongly supported that agreement in the country, that is, free wheat and flour and reduced duties on agricultural implements. I have here a comparison-I am not going to trouble the House with putting it upon the record-of the duties on agricultural implements under the reciprocity agreement and under this new proposal. So far as there is any change, this gives a greater reduction, taking them altogether, than did the reciprocity agreement, and under those conditions I am glad to support the Budget. In view of the fact that these reductions are very important considerations amongst the agricultural community, I am quite sure no hon. member representing an agricultural constituency would like to vote against this Budget, containing as it does these important proposals which he so cordially endorses.
With reference to the investigation promised next fall, I am sure every thoughtful member of the House will agree that it is absolutely necessary preceding a thorough revision of the tariff. In respect of that I have little to add to what the Minister of Immigration and Colonization so well said yesterday. I stand in respect of it exactly where my hon. friend does, but I want to emphasize one point in connection with it.

The Minister of Finance, in announcing it, said that the investigation would be conducted in such a way as to give the consumer, the producer and the workingman all an opportunity to be heard and their representations made in order that the Government might have their views. I believe that in every revision of the tariff that position is sound. The consumer's interest should be considered; the producer's interest should be considered; both should have the careful consideration of the Government. As regards men engaged in manufacturing, I believe in the past some have made great profits, no doubt contributed to by a protective tariff. I do not believe any man whose business is carried on under the protection of a tariff which enables him to increase his profits has any right to question that the legislation should be so framed and carried out as to protect both the workingman employed in his factory, and the consumer, of the goods produced. These are very important features of the proposals of the Minister of Finance.
In passing, let me say just a word on the other two matters I have mentioned as inevitable results of the war. My hon. friend opposite (Mr. Trahan) charged the Government with being responsible for the high cost of living. Who is responsible for the high cost of living in England? The Government, I suppose. Who is responsible for the high cost of living in France? My hon. friend, I am afraid, would not say the French Government, but if he is logical, he would have to do so. Who is responsible for the high cost of living in the United States? The President, no doubt. Thfe high cost of living and the increase in the cost of living were just as inevitable as casualties upon the fields of Flanders, and it is no more within the power of a government at this time to bring the cost of living back to pre-war days than it is for the Government to raise the 60,000 dead in Flanders fields. No government can make up for the diminished production or the awful war wastage of the past five years. Let us frankly face the issue. It is not possible, it cannot be done. We are paying the price of war; we are paying the price of victory. Let us whine less about paying the price when our gallant men overseas have so nobly paid it on the fields of Flanders.
You cannot wage a war like this and not pay the penalty for years after it, and I hope that the realization of the price we have to pay for the part Canada has taken
in this war will enable us to appreciate the hope, at least, that comes from the League of Nations, which we earnestly trust will be established to avoid forever a repetition of this horrible war. While the Government cannot get us back to the pre-war cost of living-no government can- I agree that everything a government can possibly do to prevent excessive profits and exorbitant prices should be done by a government. I believe that my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar) did everything which he believed-and he is a wise man on the subject-could properly be done by the Government in that direction. The Department of Labour has also been dealing with certain important aspects of the question and a Committee of the House is now investigating the whole problem.
I pass now to the third, the question of industrial unrest. Hon. members have said that the industrial unrest is due to the excessive cost of living. The excessive cost of living is not the cause of the industrial unrest; it aggravates it undoubtedly, but it is not the cause. It is very superficial thinking to say that the cost of living is the cause of the industrial unrest, and I am afraid the majority of the people of this country and even some of the members of this House are not aware of the deep and vital currents of social and economic thought that are moving the masses of the workingmen in all countries to-day. The movement had started long before the war, but the war has given it a tremendous impetus. The workingman in all lands is determined that so far as he is concerned he is going to have a better deal in the days to come than he had in the days before the war. A reduction in the cost of living will not solve the problem of industrial unrest. The worker demands vastly more. There are two currents of thought among the workers on this matter, and may I just suggest what they are. One believes in co-operation between labour and capital, and that by such co-operation the best interests of both can be secured. The other believes that there is inevitable and irreconcilable conflict between the two, and that there can be no peace until Capitalism is destroyed and a dictatorship of the proletariat established. They preach a class war. One believes in the right of private property regulated and controlled by the State, so that the workingman and citizen may own his own home, the farmer his own land; the other believes

that private ownership of property must he completely and forever destroyed. One 'believes in democracy and in the right of every citizen to an equal voice in the government of his country; the other repudiates democracy and demands the dictatorship of the proletariat. One believes in using constitutional methods for the redress of grievances and the improvement of the position of labour. The other repudiates constitutional methods and demands direct action and the use of force. One bases its claim for a change in social and economic conditions on the justice and righteousness of its cause; the other on the force at its command.
The one stands for law and order under constituted authority, the other for the overthrow of the existing form of government and the substitution therefor of the Soviet, under the dictatorship of the workers, as in Russia. One is Anglo-Saxon in its origin, democratic in its outlook, the result of the development of the labour movement under Anglo-Saxon and democratic institutions. The other is German in its origin and in its spirit. Its leaders are the disciples of Carl Marx, and proclaim economic and social theories developed under the blighting influence of German autocracy. Lenine and other disciples of Carl Marx proclaim the gospel of force and that might means right just as unblushingly as either the Kaiser or Bernhardi.
