It may surprise many people to be told that there are hundreds in Canada to-day, as there are in Great Britain, the United 'States and in all other democratic countries who hold the extreme views I have mentioned and are openly and assiduously advocating them. There is no occasion to doubt their sincerity. They advocate their views with all the energy and enthusiasm of the disciples of a militant faith. The industrial question is the most difficult and the most important problem facing the people of Canada to-day.
We have had the tariff for the past forty years discussed pro and con. No action you may take to loweT it, as between low tariff and high, will have half so great an effect on the future of Canada as will the solution of the industrial problem which we are now facing. What is true of Canada is equally true of the neighbouring republic, the United States. I have not time to read to the House the address of President Wilson at the opening of the present Congress, but he proclaims to the people of the United States that the great outstanding problem facing the people of that country is the labour problem. There is exactly the same

situation in Great Britain, exactly the same situation in France. We must face it, and how are we to solve the problem? So far as I am concerned, and I believe it is the view of the members of this House and the people of this country, having regard to the situation which exists in Canada, and the magnificent part the workers of Canada took in the war, I believe that in the days that lie before us labour should have larger recognition than it has had in the past.
They are asking certain specific things. They ask for an eight-hour day; they ask for a living wage or a larger share in the joint product of labour and capital; they ask for a larger voice in the control of industry; they ask for more adequate provision against unemployment. At the Peace Conference all these questions were fully and seriously considered, and all the statesmen of the world there assembled came to the conclusion that these demands were in spirit just, and that all nations should take steps to meet them; and I believe that in the wise dealing with this problem, in real sympathy with labour, in endeavouring to establish not a class war between labour and capital but the most hearty cooperation between the two, lies the hope of Canada for the future, and that upon that rests the peace, progress and prosperity of our country. Towards that this Government, this House, and the people of this country, employers and employees, must direct their attention.
What should we do under these conditions? There is this extreme element in Canada actively propagating the views I have mentioned. I know it. I have the responsibility of administering the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and for months I have had weekly and sometimes daily reports on the conditions. We know what these men are saying in secret. It is not necessary to 'tell you what they say in secret; it is only necessary to tell you what they say in public. At the Calgary conference to organize the One Big Union, what did that conference decide? I have the resolutions here, and I wish I had time to read them.
Read them.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Does the hon. minisetr say that both these resolutions which he has read were read and passed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the first one appears in the official report of the convention as being proposed, while the second one appears as having been passed. Take the next one:	-
Whereas holding tile belief in the ultimate supremacy of the working class in matters economic and political and that the light of modern developments have proved that the legitimate aspirations of the labor movement are repeatedly obstructed by the existing political forms, clearly showing the capitalistic nature of the parliamentary machinery.
This convention expresses its open conviction that the system of industrial soviet control by selection of representatives from industries is more efficient and of greater political value than the present system of government by selection from district.
This convention declares its full acceptance of the principle of "Proletarian Dictatorship" as being absolute and efficient for the transformation of capitalist private property to communal wealth.
The convention sends fraternal greetings to the Russian Soviet government, the Spartacans in Germany and all definite working class movements in Europe and the world recognizing they have won first place in the history of the class struggle.
Let me quote an extract from another one:
That the interests of all members of the international working class being identical that this body of workers recognize no alien but
the capitalist	Our alien, in so far as we
are concerned, that is the master clas3. that is the reason for this resolution.
Here is another one, No. 7:
Therefore be it resolved that this conference places itself on record as being in full accord and sympathy with the aims and purposes of the Russian Bolshevik and Spartacan revolutions ; and be it further resolved that this conference is in favour of calling a general strike should the Allies persist in their attempt to overthrow the Soviet administration in Russia or Germany or in any country in which it is or may be established.

Was that
passed ?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It was also adopted at the conference to organize the One Big Union movement in Western Canada, held at Calgary some few weeks ago. What I want to point out to the House and the country is that we must clearly appreciate the seriousness of the situation on the one hand, and on the other, the importance of discriminating between men seeking to overthrow constituted authority, and sober, serious leaders of the movement. A certain group of western men came to the Trades and Labour Council's annual meeting held, I think, in the city of Quebec last September or October, and sought to press these radical views upon the body of labour there, and the sober, serious leaders of labour at that conference fought the resolutions and defeated them. I do not mean, of course, these particular resolutions, but the radical resolutions that were then submitted. What did the men of the West who presented

these radical resolutions do? They went West and organized this One Big Union movement to cut adrift from the sober leaders of the East and from men like Samuel Gompers and other great leaders of organized labour in the United States Why did they cut adrift? Because they knew that under the serious and judicious leadership of the men who made the labour movement what it is in Canada and the United States they could not advocate the overthrow of constituted authority without incurring the hostility of these men. The quesion is asked: Why do you not take action? Well, I believe that the only way in which you oan successfully defeat error is by teaching the truth; the only way in which you can combat false ideas is by promulgating true ones. And I think it is of the utmost importance that the people of this country who do believe in organized government, who do believe in democratic government, and who are' not prepared that the Russian Soviet system, with all that it implies, shall be introduced into Canada, should make clear their views on these issues and le.t the public know and understand what is involved in them. The same convention that stood by the Soviet form of government demanded free speech and liberty of action in Canada.
Are you opposed to that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Am I opposed to it ? The fact that these men moved these resolutions and carried them unmolested is the best evidence of the absolute freedom of speech in Canada. Now, in Russia there is no freedom of speech. In Russia there is no freedom of the press. In Russia there is no freedom of assembly. In Russia there is no right to vote except by the workers who support the Soviet Bolshevik movement.
Mr. CANNON. The same as here?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has the right to vote. Does he say he is a supporter of the Russian Bolshevik movement? There they only permit men to vote who work with their hands. The man who works with his brain has no right to vote over there. My hon. friend will be able to say in which class he belongs under that classification. They have no freedom of speech, no freedom of the press and no right of assembly. No man except those who will absolutely support the Bolshevik movement has a right to vote. They dis-

solved the constitutional assembly because it did not support the minority. They stand for a dictatorship of a limited class. They stand for the dictatorship of a limited class, a fraction of the population of Russia, who exercise their power in as despotic a manner as the Government of the Czar. Do the people want anything like that in Canada? That is the result in Russia. There is no question about it. These people cannot triumph in Canada. The sober, serious-thinking people of this country will stand by constituted authority. The people who own their own property will not stand for confiscation. In Russia they take the furniture of a man in the city, the live stock and agricultural implements of the farmer, and they make them the property of the community. The people of this country will not stand for those theories and practices. The man who within this House or this country delivers inflammatory speeches charging the Government with profiteering and being friends of the profiteers is playing into the hands of these very Bolsheviks, and it would only be a certain measure of justice if the first property confiscated were his and he were put to do the manual labour that is required in Russia. These people say they want freedom. I gathered from the remarks of my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe)that he had rather a liking and sympathy for his friends of the Soviet government.
Oh, no; not at all, but I want freedom of speech.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend will not get what he wants, because there is no freedom of speech in Russia and they entorce compulsory military service there.
It is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rowell) who is in sympathy with that part of their programme.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am certainly a believer in compulsory military service in time of war, and that it is the duty of every man to defend 'his country in the hours of his country's need. We must combat ideas with ideas. There is another thing we must do. It is the first duty of every Government in Canada, municipal, provincial and federal, to see that law and order are preserved and that life and property are protected. There has been a great popular misconception-I do not know what is the explanation of it-that the federal Government is the only Government that has power to act. One would think from the way some people talk

in this House and outside of it, and from the way that some newspapers write, that we had a legislative union, instead of a federal union in Canada, that this Government has all the authority, that the provinces and municipalities have none, and that if any trouble arises the only thing to do is to send to this Government and ask them to right it. Then, if this Government does not immediately right it, it is damned and said to be no good. To illustrate: They had trouble out in a small community in British Columbia. They had a strike. There were some aliens misconducting themselves. The Acting Prime Minister got a telegram from the chairman of the committee of the town asking the Federal Government to intervene and to preserve life and property in that town. What answer did he send back? He said: Have you applied to the Provincial Government for protection? If you have applied to the Provincial Government and they say they need Federal assistance, the Federal Government will' immediately come to your aid. That is the Federal constitution. The provinces are extremely jealous of their rights at times, they are very jealous of their autonomy at times; but when it comes to dealing with disagreeable tasks, they are prepared to shift their responsibility to the Federal Government and throw their sins upon us. It cannot be too clearly stated that the responsibility for maintaining law and order rests in the first instance upon the municipal government. If they are able to maintain law and order the responsibility rests upon them. If they are unable to preserve law and order, the law contains provisions whereby they may call to their assistance other forces. Next to the municipal government the responsibility rests upon the Provincial Government. They are responsible for the administration of justice and for the prosecution of offenders against the law. If there is any failure
10 p.m. to prosecute any man for any offence under the law the responsibility rests upon the Provincial Government. It does not rest with this Government. The policy of this Government is this: If municipalities find that they are unequal to the task, or if the provinces find themselves unequal to the task, of preserving law and order, this Government is prepared to back them up to the full limit of its power.
I appeal to the members of this House; if you hear criticisms of the Government in connection with these matters, find out first what the municipal or provincial authorities have done. First, have they done their
duty? It is not until they have called upon the Federal Government for assistance that we have the right or the duty to intervene.
One word further as to what we should do. I think we must meet this labour situation fairly and squarely. We must do justice, and more than justice to the legitimate demands of labour. We must put the honest, patriotic, public-spirited labour leaders into a position to successfully combat the extremists in their own ranks by showing that the Government and people of this country have dealt fairly and squarely with them.	We have to deal fairly
and squarely with labour and we have to maintain law and order.
I know of no other panacea. As I view the situation-.and I believe it is true in every democratic country in the world- important as may be the tariff, the great issue facing the governments to-day is the problem of labour and the industrial issue. On the wise and patriotic solution of this problem depends the hope for the peace, progress and prosperity of the countries involved.
May I close by referring again to the tariff. I believe that, for Canada, more important that any particular scale of tariff duties is a good understanding between East and West and all sections of Canada. No section can 'have its own way absolutely, and unity and strength be our portion. Confederation was brought about by the public-spirited leaders in those days recognizing that something must be surrendered in order to obtain the greater end, the greater goodwill, and to bring about a united Canada. I say to the manufacturers in the East and to the farmers in the West, and in every other section of the country Canada can only be strong and prosperous, she can only prove worthy of the gallant sons who have died for the right if we try to get together, not press our prejudices or even our convictions to the issue, but unite whole-heartedly as a public-spirited Canadian people in enacting legislation which we can all co-operate in working out and which will make for the unity and strength of this great and growing nation.

Mr. Speaker, the papers of this country have been printing rumours as to a probable election. I was very much in doubt as to whether the Government would decide to go to the country or not till I heard the speech delivered by the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) who evidently is training for the stump. I can only say that if he repeats on the hustings the

speech that he has made to-night, he may achieve an oratorical success, but the people after pondering upon it may say: " It was a beautiful shell, hut a very empty one indeed."
A few weeks ago during a debate here I mentioned my fear that a revolution was threatening in Canada. As a result 1 have read in the papers that as usual I was an extremist,, that as usual I had spoiled my speech by making a statement which had no foundation in fact. To-night I heard the President of the Privy Council make a far more serious statement, and one which he supports with all the responsibility of a Cabinet position. The President of the Privy Council has declared to the House and to the country that not only are we threatened with a revolution but that the revolution is an actuality. Mr. Speaker, I am very much afraid that the revolution might not be as actual as the minister has depicted it, but the war in Europe being over he feels it is necessary to have a small local war so as to permit him to repeat his familiar arguments.
The minister was very severe in his account of the situation in Russia. He described the programme of the Bolshevik party in full detail. I am curious to know where the minister got his information? Is it perchance from newspapers that are prohibited?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I got the information
from official documents issued by the British Government, a copy of which was laid on the table of the House a short time ago.

I see, the minister gets
his knowledge from the first cousin to his own Information Bureau. Let me say to him that if the situation in Russia is so serious, if the programme of the Bolsheviki is such as has'been described by him, how is it that this Government has withdrawn the 'Canadian troops sent to Siberia? Those troops were, or were not, sent for a purpose. If they were sent for no purpose the Government has committed a blunder and has made a mistake. If the troops were sent to put down the Bolshevik movement, and if it was necessary to suppress that movement, why has the Government recalled those troops?
Mr. Speaker, I had always read of the minister as being the leader of the Liberal party in the province of Ontario up to the year 1917 when he joined the Union Government. Listening to his speech tonight, I have noticed that the former Liberal provincial leader has become a great Canadian Tory. He has a good word for the

profiteer, and for the manufacturer, but a bad word for the aspirations of labour-in short, he has spoken as very few Tories would dare to speak in this country. As a Liberal who still remains what he was two years ago; as a Liberal who has not forgotten Liberal principles, I believe there will be very little regret over his departure from our ranks. The rest of his speech was a very eloquent exposition of what I have already read in the Canadian Official Record. I am not surprised that the President of the Privy Council approves of the Budget. If he did not so approve he would not be where he is, and most probably that approval is due to his desire to retain his present position. Neither am I surprised that the minister disapproves of the stand taken by the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar). That - hon. gentleman has left the Cabinet, a thing the President of the Privy Council will never do, I am quite sure.
* Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Marquette stated his position on the tariff, and the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) gave him the answer from the Government benches. This reminded me of an incident in the history of France when Marshal Ney-that hero, " the bravest of the brave," who had faced the enemies of his country on many battlefields of Europe, from the sunny plains of Portugal to the frozen banks of the Beresina, was brought to trial, the then King of France, Louis XVIII, moved no doubt by an extreme feeling of Bourbonic malice, called upon the fellow marshals of this great soldier to preside at his trial and to send him to his doom. The Premier of this country, moved by a spirit worthy of Machiavelli, yesterday called on a brother member from the West, an intimate political friend of the member for Marquette, to criticise the latter's conduct and to cast suspicion upon his motives. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization went through the ordeal very successfully. His personal friendship, and his political intimacy, gave way before an ardent desire to show his complete and entire subservience to his master. Such achievements, Mr. Speaker, are only natural to men of a certain class. In 1917, many Liberals in Canada left the banners of Sir Wilfrid Laurier from motives of real patriotism, although I think they were misguided. Others left the Old Chieftain because of lower motives. Time-servers they were by instinct, politicians they were by nature, and it is here that I come back to the Minister of Colonization and Immigration.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. gentleman is entirely exceeding his privileges in attributing unworthy motives to an hon. member of this House. It is scarcely in conformity with the dignity of the House that he should do so.

Mr. Speaker, I bow to
your decision and say that others were moved by motives of less high order. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization in a speech which he delivered yesterday said that he was moved by only one consideration, and that consideration was the dictates of his conscience.
Mr. -Speaker, evidently the conscience of a man is beyond the judgment and the criticism of his neighbour. It is impossible to gauge the inner recesses of a man's conscience-I will not attempt to do it. But, on the other hand, we can always judge a man's motives by his acts. The Minister of Immigration and Colonization said that he was moved by his conscience. Was he moved by his conscience when, in the spring of 1917, Mr. Speaker, he was organizing throughout the Western Provinces a system to turn out of power the Government presided over by his actual chief? What were the dictates of the hon. gentleman's conscience when he was sending to the Liberal organization ways and means of putting out a government that he considered corrupt and absolutely unworthy of directing the affairs of this country? Conscience, the minister said, Mr. Speaker. Had the dictates of his conscience altered, when, at the convention at Winnipeg, he was drafting resolutions to the effect that the right hon. gentleman who is at the head of this Government was unworthy of being Prime Minister of this country? Conscience, the minister said, Mr. Speaker. Were the motives and the dictates of the hon. gentleman's conscience the same as they are today when he sent to the Prime Minister a message saying that no. Union Government *was to be considered with the right hon. gentleman at its head. Conscience, the hon. gentleman said, Mr. Speaker. When the War-time Elections Act was passed, when it was obvious to any observer that the Liberal party had no more chance in the Prairie Provinces, the hon. gentleman jumped on the first train and rushed to Ottawa, and on his knees he crept into the gilded hole wherein he has remained since -always with his conscience, Mr. Speaker. Conscience ! Mr. Speaker, I would like the hon. gentleman to explain to this House how the dictates of his conscience would permit him, whilst he was a member of this
Union Cabinet, to come down to the city of Quebec, and to other cities within our province, to try to make new readjustments and rearrangements to put out of power the Government to which he belongs. Conscience ! Mr. Speaker. Did hisi conscience dictate the correspondence which he sent to the various political leaders of this country in order to organize a movement which would put this Government from power? Mr. Speaker, I leave the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization to his conscience, but I must say, before concluding, that up to now the uncrowned king of the western renegades was Clifford Sifton; I think that his crewn and his kingship are now in danger.
Julius Caesar had no press agent-or rather, Julius Caesar was his own press agent. The hon. leader of this Government, although no less a man, is more fortunate a ruler, for he has a whole galaxy of sycophants who describe to the astounded universe his exceptionally high achievements. The hon. President of the Privy Council, who has just taken his seat, with his well-fed helpmates, Mr. Dafoe and his very faithful scribblers, have described, so as to enthuse the native Canadians and arouse their patriotic fervour, the Peace Conference as a world stage where our Prime Minister, surrounded by the dazzling and witty Mr. Doherty, the fascinating Mr. Foster, and the idealistic Mr. Sifton, has dictated in a stern tone of voice the terms of everlasting peace to prostrate Germany; coaching Wilson; advising Lloyd George; counselling Clemenceau; helping along Orlando. Even that did not satisfy the boundless energies of our Prime Minister. His omnipotent influence spread to the war-torn Balkan states. To Russia he went, and on the remote shores of Prinkipo island he stood, the bearer of a message of conciliation to the sturdy sons of Gengis Khan and the blood-stained followers of Lenine. But, Mr. Speaker, enough of this ridiculous camouflage, enough of this grotesque business. The Prime Minister of our country had as much to do with the readjustment of European affairs as the hon. member for Digby and Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) has to do with lowering of the cost of living.
What has been the result of this Peace Conference, Mr. Speaker, as far as Canada is concerned? What have we gained? Every country whose representatives sat around the Peace Table has obtained something. England will have Egypt, she will have new territories in Asia, and she will have

part of the German colonies. Every other part of the British Empire has secured some advantage. South Africa will have some of the German colonies; Australia will have some islands, and New Zealand will also acquire new territory. And what will we get? If we get anything, Mr. Speaker, it will he a chunk of icy Greenland.
Not only has every country acquired territorial advantages, but huge indemnities are to be paid. How much will we receive? Since his return the Prime Minister has made but one statement in this House; it was in connection with the Winnipeg strike. The matter was important, I will admit, Mr. Speaker; but there is a more important matter before this country, the matter of whether we are to get something from the war, whether we are to secure some advantage from the Peace Conference. As to that the Prime Minister has remained' silent, and I have no doubt, will continue to remain silent. Why should we not have a part of this indemnity? Have we not spent enough money, have we not made enough sacrific? The sacred remains of our dead over in France, Mr. Speaker, the mangled limbs of our wounded, the victories of our battalions, the abnegation of our civil population, give us a valid claim to obtain fair and proportionate compensation for our important and vast outlay.
But in connection with this matter, as in connection with many others, we read beautiful articles in the press, we were told that our Prime Minister had attained the very highest heights of Imperial statesmanship-but he comes back empty handed, with nothing to offer to the people of this country.
As a Canadian who loves fair play, and as an Irishman who cherishes the memory of O'Connell and Parnell, I wish to protest against the indifference shown by our peace delegates to the cause of Irish freedom. The Government cannot unfetter the Poles, the Government cannot unshackle the Slovaks, the Government cannot deliver the Czechs, and at the one and same time trample under foot the national aspirations of a loyal and generous nation. Love of liberty is a gift given to man by God, and no human power, no matter how strong it may be, can wring from the heart of an Irishman the desire he has to see his country free like every other country in the world. Providence has moulded for the sons of St. Patrick a noble future, and the laws of Providence and also the laws of outraged humanity insist and imperatively demand that fair play should prevail. I

regret that at this Peace Conference the man who is supposed to represent the Irish population of Canada in this .Cabinet, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), has forgotten to that extent his duty towards Ireland and his compatriots as not to utter one word to help our glorious cause, not to utter one sentence to promote a sacred cause, that of Irish freedom.
At this late hour, I do not wish to detain the House very long, but I should like to say a few words in connection with the financial situation of Canada, as described by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). I admired the minister for his frankness. He told the people where we were, how deeply we were in debt and how enormous were our liabilities. For his frankness and his sincerity I thank and congratulate him, but I wish to touch on one subject in connection with our finances. How is it that our situation is so poor? How is it that our debt is so high? How is it, in a word, that Canada is in such a mess? The first reason is- our past extravagance. From 1911 to 1914, before the war, and from 1914 to 1917, since the outbreak of war, the Government of this country has run things in a most extravagant way. I regret that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) is not in his seat. I should' like to have his facility of speech and his eloquence to denounce the scandals of government extravagance in the way he did in connection, for instance, with the Allison scandal. I should like to have his information and parliamentary experience to show to the members of this House and to the people of this country at large how extravagant, how careless, this Government has been. Past extravagance is one of the causes of our bad financial situation, and when I see the Minister of Public Works in this Cabinet, I can say to him what the Bishop of Paris said to the chief of a barbarian army: "Convert yourself to Christianity, and if you wish to give evidence of your sincerity and of your good faith, burn what you have worshipped; worship what you have burned." The sooner the Minister of Public Works burns what he has been worshipping for the past two years, the better for himself, the better for this country and the batter foT everybody concerned. But I may add that if the minister does not wish to burn what he has been worshipping for the last two years, we shall leave him alone in his gilded temple of paganism where he now is, muttering insincere prayers to an

irresponsive divinity and offering to the Golden Calf the shattered remains of his former principles.
Past extravagance has been the cause of our bad financial situation. Future extravagance will aggravate our financial liabilities and will heighten, if possible, the huge pile of our national obligations. What does this Government propose? The Government proposes a new shipbuilding policy. I do not wish to criticise, the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), but I wish to criticise the enormous amounts which are being spent at the present time in shipbuilding. We ought to wait; we ought to curtail our expenditure. If there is one good feature about my hon. friend's policy it is this, that he wishes to have Canadian shipbuilding and a Canadian navy. Whenever this Government does anything good, that good it borrows from the programme of our late lamented leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and when the Minister of Naval Affairs propounded his programme of a naval policy, it was to the grave of our late leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that he went and plucked the seed of Canada's future naval greatness.
Let me take, as another example of extravagance, the policy of the Government as regards railways. We are unloading on to the people of this country the enormous debts of the Canadian Northern railway and of Mackenzie & Mann, and we have the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid), who is now going to be the president or the head or the inspiring spirit of a new huge railway combination-and I am quite sure, judging by the speeches the minister has made in this House, judging by the ability and cleverness he has shown before the members of this assembly, that Shaughnessy will pale into insignificance and Beatty vanish into nothingness.
The unrest which exists everywhere throughout Canada to-day has been discussed by hon. members who have preceded me in this debate, and I do not wish to dwell at great length on that subject. Briefly, the first class of people in this country who are dissatisfied, are the farmers. The farmers want a low tariff; they want better trade conditions; they want to be helped by this Government, but the Government refuses to help them. The farmers from the West, the farmers from Ontario, and the farmers from the East, have united in one demand for a lower tariff on food stuffs and agricultural implements. I admit that the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance makes certain reductions, but it does not meet the legitimate demands of the farmers. As long as this Government is more concerned with the interest of the manufacturer and of the industrial concerns than with the interests of the farming class, unrest among the farmers will continue to exist, and it will not disappear or abate until justice is done to them.
The second class of people in this country who are dissatisfied are the returned soldiers. And why? They fought on the other side and won a glorious victory. When they come back here what do they receive? Beautiful speeches of welcome, magnificent addresses, eloquent orations. Words, Mr. Speaker, words again, and always words; never, or very seldom, deeds.
I am not the only one to condemn the attitude of the Government towards the returned soldier. Sitting upon your right is an hon. member who has always been a supporter of this Government, who resigned from his position as Parliamentary Secretary for the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment because the Government would not do anything for the returned soldier, because it was neglecting the most elementary and essential function of the Government in this vital and fundamental matter. More than that, a few days ago Lieutenant-Colonel McKelvey Bell resigned from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. These are the things that show us that the returned soldiers have real grievances, and that these grievances will not be removed by this Government unless its policy is changed, and changed completely.
The third class of people in this country who are dissatisfied are the workingmen. I heard the President of the Privy Council reading to-night resolutions moved by extremists at labour conferences throughout Canada. I am not concerned with what the extremists among the workingmen of this country want, but I am concerned with what the ordinary workingman of this country demands. What does he demand ? Only one thing; he demands fair play and equal justice. The workingmen of this country contributed the greater portion of the military contingents that we sent to Europe. When the workingman was in the trenches of France or Flanders he was equal to the manufacturer, the rich man, and the millionaire. To-day he comes back to Canada and he wants the equality to be preserved. He wants no more class privileges in this country, and no more class legislation. He wants his rights to he acknowledged and

.1418

recognized just as the rights and privileges of the capitalists have been acknowledged and recognized for years. I read in the papers to-day that riots took place in the city of Winnipeg yesterday and that numerous people were wounded, among them a soldier who had won high distinction in France and returned to this country decorated with the Victoria Cross. Unfortunately, his wound is .probably mortal! Why is this strike in Winnipeg not settled? What does the labouring man in Winnipeg demand? He demands a very simple thing. The metal workers of Winnipeg want their union recognized. Why should it not be recognized? At the Peace Conference in Paris the Premier of this country subscribed to the covenant regarding labour legislation for the future, and one of the fundamental proposals agreed upon was that the rights of labour to organize into unions should be recognized throughout the world. Why should this be denied in the city of Winnipeg when it is proclaimed in Paris, and has received the signature of the Prime Minister of this country as representing the Canadian people? The President of the Privy Council said this evening that the people of Canada believed that the provinces have no more rights. Certainly the people of Canada believe that, and why? Because this Government, during a period of four years, has deprived the provinces of every right given to them under the constitution. Orders in Council have been passed, and legislation has been enacted, and every particle of privilege and right has been taken away from the provinces. Is it then extraordinary to-day that the people of this country, after such a reign of autocracy by the Federal Government, should doubt whether the provinces had any rights? The President of the Privy Council says that the provinces are to settle these labour troubles. I take issue with him there. I say that the Federal Government at Ottawa, under the British North America Act, has the right to legislate in everything that concerns public order in this country. Labour unrest is against public order, and to remedy the condition of affairs that exists throughout Canada to-day the Federal Government should take advantage of that provision in the British North America Act and bring down legislation that will bring rest where there is unrest to-day.
But what can we expect from this Government? We have been sitting here for six months-I should have said four months, but it seemed to me like six-and what

legislation has been brought down? The Government thought of themselves at first, and the main legislation they brought down was the Bankruptcy Bill. We were told during the debate on the Address that we had to reconstruct this country, that questions of the greatest importance had to be solved. But no legislation was brought down. Then we were told that we had to await the return of the Prime Minister from France. The right hon. gentleman has returned, and what legislation has been brought down since? To-day we are told that next week we shall have three sittings a day so that we can get hqme as soon as possible.	[DOT]
No wonder the people are not satisfied. Who would be satisfied? It is useless discussing the. high cost of living; it is useless discussing profiteering; and it is useless discussing various other reasons for the unrest that prevails. The main reason for the dissatisfaction of the people is the fact that we have still at the head of our affairs m Canada the Government that has bungled through eight years of administration. The moment this Government disappears 75 per cent of the discontent in this country will disappear with it.
The fourth class of people who are dissatisfied jn this country are the consumers. The President of the Privy Council asserted quite solemnly that the cost of living could not be reduced. The Hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) was in his seat when that statement was made; several other members of the Cabinet were also in their places. None of them protested; therefore, the President of the Privy Council when he uttered those words expressed the opinion of the Cabinet. Now the Government considers that nothing can be done to lower the cost of living. This is the consoling message -which the President.of the Privy Council has to offer the people of Canada. Starving women in our cities, suffering men and suffering children who have been looking for comfort and a remedy to this deplorable condition of things, have received from the President of the Privy Council the reassuring information that nothing can be done! Mr. Speaker, if the President of the Privy Council and the Government are convinced that nothing, can be done to effect a reduction in the cost of living in Canada, how is it, may I ask, that last week it was decided to appoint a committee of the House to consider the subject with a view to discovering some means of lowering the cost of living? Is the Government merely trying to deceive the

[DOT]3419
people? What is this committee doing? The committee is investigating conditions in fcanada and will probably present a report; but the Government beforehand declares to the country that nothing can be done in the matter. Are they serious? I have very little experience in Parliament, but I must say that never have I seen in any parliament or read in any book on parliamentary events the case of a- government appointing a committee to investigate conditions in a country, and after having appointed that committee, and while the committee was at work, a member of the Cabinet declaring on behalf of the Government that it was useless to attempt to remedy such a condition of things as that which now exists in Canada. But we knew beforehand that the President of the Privy Council would take no steps to lower the cost of living in this country. The President of the Council is too generous and warm-hearted to cause any pain to his bosom friend, Sir Joseph Flavelle. They adore God in the same church; they offer to Heaven prayers in common. They modestly bow their heads before Divinity and in all humility kiss the dust of earth and say: How small we are when we are in church, but how big when we are outside. I am not surprised that the Government will do nothing to decrease the profits of the profiteers. The profiteers have put this Government into power; they have subscribed the money to put them where they are. Every member of the Government represents a body which is indebted to the profiteers of this country, and human nature is such that the attitude of men to heavy creditors is at the least that of extreme politeness.
The Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder), following in the footsteps of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sif-ton)-our idealistic Peace delegate, as I said, while the minister was away-said that, although he did not approve of the principle of protection he would support the Budget and remain in the Cabinet. I appeal to your parliamentary experience, Sir, and to your knowledge of constitutional usage. Has there ever been heard in any British parliament or in any parliament where British constitutional procedure is 'followed a member of the Governement making such a declaration? If you will permit me, for the benefit of the hon. Minister of Immigration, I will give a very short history of the constitution so far as this question is concerned. A ministry never existed in England before William III, and if you will read the splendid essay by Sir
217i
William Temple you will see laid down the first principles of a ministry and also of a cabinet. The Whigs came into power under William III, and for the first time there was a ministry in England. Further development brought on a cabinet. Under the Georges this cabinet was more or less regular and complete. But under William IV and under Queen Victoria the cabinet assumed the form in which it is at present in England and in every other British country. What is the cabinet? The cabinet is the union of a small number of men, sitting either in the Lower or in the Upper House, who advise the King direct or through the Governor General on questions of policy and who agree together and necessarily must agree together. Not only are the members of the Cabinet bound to agree on every question submitted to Parliament but every member of that Cabinet is responsible for the acts of his colleagues. That is, there must not only be ministerial responsibility, but there must be a responsible solidarity. How, in this country, can a minister declare in Parliament that he is not in favour of a policy of the Government, but nevertheless will approve of the Government and remain in the Cabinet? Mr. Speaker, these are elementary principles. The Government during the war cast aside every precedent we knew in this country; but now, to suit their purpose, ministers make speeches of a nature to remove the corner stone of responsible government. I do not think that the people of the country will tolerate such an attitude. Ministers must approve a policy of the Government in principle and in its entirety. If they do not they must leave the cabinet. Instances are numerous in support of this doctrine. Just consider, Eir, what happened in England. Probably in England the people are more careful in the matter of constitutional precedent than is the hon. Minister of Customs. At the opening of the war, members on principle left the Government led by the Hon. Mr. Asquith because they did not see eye to eye with the Prime 'Minister. As they did not see eye to eye with the Premier they were bound, according to constitutional precedent, to leave the Cabinet. John Burns, a poor man, gave up his portfolio and the emoluments of office to save his principles. Morley did the same thing, and more recently Lord Robert Cecil dropped from the Lloyd George Cabinet because he did not approve in principle of the policy laid down by the Government. These are actions held up to the admiration of people

who like British institutions. I will ask the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, when they have any leisure time, to study these precedents. If they do ithey may, revise their views.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude. Charles V, King of Spain, Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, after having lighted the fires of religious warfare throughout Europe, abdicated his tottering throne and withdrew into a convent, where he used to meditate on the vanity of all things human. Rumour has it that the Right Hon. the Prime Minister of this country (Sir Robert Borden) will soon abdicate his uncertain and shaky sceptre and withdraw to the ambassadorial splendours of Washington, where he will be in a position to contemplate the disorder which he has created in his own country. May he very soon convene his faithful to the parting scene. The people of this country will fervently pray that he may take along, as members of his ambassadorial staff, his tools of evil and mates of incompetency.
On the motion of Sir Thomas White the House adjourned at 11 p.m.
Friday, June 13, 1919.
